This study investigates the generalization error of two-layer neural networks used to solve high-dimensional Schrödinger eigenvalue problems. We demonstrate that the generalization error converges at a rate of $O(N^{-1/2})$ with high probability, where $N$ represents the count of data points. Furthermore, under specific conditions, we establish that the generalization error is bounded above by $O(N^{-1/2})$. These findings are derived using the localized Rademacher complexity framework. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical results. The source code for this work is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2000000000/Apriori-NN-Schrodinger}. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a prominent class of machine learning models designed to process sequential data. This study examines their efficacy in modeling neuronal activity within the nematode *C. elegans*. We demonstrate that RNNs can accurately replicate both the temporal dynamics and the correlations between neurons in this organism. Furthermore, we explore the application of these models to infer synaptic connections, revealing that while they fail to reconstruct the complete synaptic graph, they successfully identify a significant subset of connections. Finally, we show that RNNs can predict neuronal responses to novel stimuli, indicating their potential utility for forecasting neuronal behavior. These findings suggest that RNNs serve as a valuable tool for analyzing neuronal time series data. The accompanying code and data are accessible at https://github.com/NeuroML/2020_RNNs_Celegans. Additionally, the paper includes a supplementary section detailing the experimental setup, which outlines the data collection process, the construction of the synaptic graph, and the generation of neuronal responses to stimuli. We demonstrate that the fixed point forest of the two-dimensional Ising model adheres to a specific constraint: the ratio of the number of vertices with degree $2k$ to the number of vertices with degree $2k+1$ approaches $1$ as $k$ tends to infinity. This result is achieved by establishing an asymptotic relationship between the generating functions of these two vertex degree counts. Furthermore, we show that the generating function for the number of vertices with degree $2k+1$ can be expressed as a product of generating functions related to the local configurations of vertices with degree $2k+1$. Leveraging this relationship, we derive an asymptotic formula for the generating function of vertices with degree $2k+1$ and subsequently prove the aforementioned constraint. Additionally, we provide an asymptotic expression for the generating function regarding vertices with degree $2k$. Finally, we present a conjecture concerning the local constraint of the fixed point forest for the two-dimensional Ising model. Specifically, we propose that the ratio of vertices with degree $2k$ to those with degree $2k+1$ converges to $1$ as $k$ approaches infinity, and that the ratio of vertices with degree $2k+1$ to those with degree $2k+2$ converges to $2$ as $k$ approaches infinity. We also offer a partial proof supporting this conjecture. Our findings are applicable to the fixed point forests of the two-dimensional Ising model on the square lattice, as well as to the fixed point forests of the 3- and 4-coloring models on the triangular and square lattices, respectively. In these cases, the local constraints are identical to those of the two-dimensional Ising model. Consequently, our results confirm the local constraints for the fixed point forests of the 3- and 4-coloring models on the triangular and square lattices, respectively. Finally, we extend our findings to the fixed point forests of the Ising model on any two-dimensional lattice, thereby proving the local constraint for these models. Additionally, we identify the irreducible representations that generate these pairs. As a corollary, we derive the complete list of robust Gelfand pairs for $GL(2,q)$, with $q$ representing a prime power. Furthermore, we determine all subgroups of $SL(2,p)$ that act robustly on the group. This research extends the findings of the authors' previous work, which covered the case when the group is $SL(2,5)$. Our methodology relies on the classification of irreducible representations and their associated characters, alongside the application of Gelfand pairs. This approach also facilitates the classification of robust Gelfand pairs for $SL(2,5)$. The study concludes with an appendix detailing the character tables for $SL(2,p)$ where $p \leq 11$. This appendix is essential for verifying the validity of our results. This study examines the electromagnetic properties of the recently observed hidden-charm molecular pentaquark states $P_{cs}(4459)$ and $P_{cs}(4338)$, which possess single strangeness. By calculating their electromagnetic form factors, we derive the corresponding charges and radii for these particles. Furthermore, we analyze their potential signatures within the reactions $\bar{D}^* N \to P_{cs} \pi$ and $\bar{D} N \to P_{cs} \gamma$. Our findings indicate that the cross sections for these processes are substantial, suggesting that the electromagnetic characteristics of $P_{cs}$ states could be investigated in future experiments. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for understanding the internal structure of $P_{cs}$ states. Finally, we compare our predictions with existing experimental data and discuss the broader implications of our conclusions. Zinbiel algebras, which serve as the duals of Novikov algebras, are defined by the Zinbiel identity. This paper demonstrates that every Zinbiel algebra is solvable. Consequently, it follows that every Novikov algebra is nilpotent. These findings provide an affirmative resolution to a question posed by D. Valiev and V. Tolstoy in their 2019 paper, "Zinbiel algebras," published in the Journal of Algebra (Volume 520, pages 1–13). Furthermore, this result establishes the optimality of the bound found in V. Tolstoy's 2018 work, "Nilpotent Zinbiel algebras," also in the Journal of Algebra (Volume 500, pages 1–10). The proofs rely on the observation that any Zinbiel algebra can be decomposed into a direct sum of indecomposable algebras. Additionally, the study examines the Zinbiel identity within the context of Lie superalgebras. It is shown that this identity holds in the supercommutator of any Lie superalgebra, implying that the identity is satisfied by the enveloping superalgebra of any Lie superalgebra. This conclusion aligns with a result by V. Tolstoy, who demonstrated that the Novikov identity is similarly satisfied in the enveloping algebra of any Lie algebra. Finally, the paper presents an example of a Zinbiel algebra that is not nilpotent. The examples provided are constructed using the method of central extensions. This study examines the three-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring a cubic nonlinear term and an inverse-square potential. We demonstrate that the associated linear evolution operator defines an isometry within the space $L^2_{x}$. Furthermore, we establish local well-posedness for the nonlinear problem in $L^2_{x}$ and prove global well-posedness within the higher-regularity space $H^{s}_{x}$ where $s>\frac{3}{4}$. The primary instrument employed is the Morawetz estimate. Additionally, we derive the scattering result for this equation. Our methodology relies on the Morawetz estimate, the Strauss radial cutoff, and the uniform Strichartz estimate. Finally, we show that the scattering theory fails to hold in the critical space $H^{\frac{3}{2}}_{x}$. This work extends the findings of Burq, Zhang, and Takaishi to encompass heterogeneous nonlinearities. The paper concludes with an appendix detailing the necessary estimates. Notably, the techniques developed here are applicable to a broader class of nonlinearities. Finally, we outline several open questions regarding this subject. This paper examines a migration model featuring two countries, each with a fixed labor force, where migration flows are driven by wage disparities. The model incorporates two spillover effects: first, an increase in Country A's wages reduces its migration to Country B, while simultaneously boosting Country B's migration from Country A and raising Country B's wages; second, the resulting migration shift increases Country A's unemployment rate, which in turn lowers Country A's wages. This dynamic creates a feedback loop where initial wage differences trigger a chain reaction of migration and wage adjustments across both nations. The study analyzes the stability of this system and the long-term impacts of these interactions. Furthermore, it explores how the model's parameters influence the system's behavior and evaluates the model's applicability to real-world migration scenarios. Finally, the paper proposes a method for calibrating the parameters using real-world data. The analysis reveals that while the model can be calibrated to actual data, the resulting parameters often produce unrealistic outcomes. Consequently, the authors conclude that the model's assumptions are too restrictive to accurately represent real-world migration dynamics. Additionally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for policymakers. The study demonstrates that the model's parameters are highly sensitive to initial wage differences, meaning that even minor disparities can lead to significant shifts in migration flows. This suggests that policies aimed at reducing wage gaps could be highly effective in mitigating migration. However, the authors also note that the model's simplifications may limit its ability to capture the full complexity of migration, and they recommend that policymakers consider a broader range of factors when designing migration policies. Finally, the paper highlights the model's potential for future research, particularly in exploring the impact of other factors such as cultural differences, family reunification, and education on migration flows. By addressing these additional variables, researchers can develop more comprehensive models that better reflect the multifaceted nature of migration. Ultimately, the authors emphasize the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration between economists, sociologists, and policymakers to gain a deeper understanding of migration dynamics and to develop effective policies that address the needs of both migrants and host countries. By fostering such collaboration, stakeholders can work together to create policies that promote social cohesion, economic growth, and human rights for all involved. Ultimately, the authors conclude that a holistic approach to migration policy is essential for achieving sustainable and equitable outcomes. By considering the perspectives and needs of all stakeholders, policymakers can develop policies that address the complex challenges of migration and contribute to a more just and inclusive society. K2-138b, a super-Earth located in the habitable zone of its host star, is hypothesized to lead a chain of three additional planets locked in a 3:2 mean motion resonance. This study aims to validate the existence of these inner planets by analyzing the radial velocity data from the HARPS-N instrument. We employed a generalized least-squares method to model the observations, yielding a best-fit solution that includes the K2-138b signal. Our analysis confirms the presence of a second planet with a minimum mass of 1.8 Earth masses and an orbital period of 10.1 days. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system's radial velocity semi-amplitudes align with a 3:2 mean motion resonance chain. These findings support the hypothesis that K2-138b is part of a resonant chain, suggesting that the formation and evolution of such systems may be more common than previously believed. Additionally, we calculated the orbital stability of the system using the N-body integrator REBOUND, finding that the system remains stable over a timescale of 100 million years. Finally, we determined the dynamical masses of the planets, resulting in values of 1.8 and 1.5 Earth masses for the two innermost planets. These results indicate that the K2-138 system is a promising candidate for future atmospheric studies. The data used in this work are accessible at https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-4339/20214251. This duality connects equivariant sheaves with equivariant modules over the equivariant quantum affine algebra, where the equivariant parameters correspond to the coweights of the general linear group. This result extends the classical quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality, which is a specific instance where equivariant parameters are set to zero. Additionally, we provide an affine version of the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality. In this context, equivariant sheaves are replaced by sheaves on the affine flag variety, equivariant quantum affine modules are substituted with modules over the quantum affine algebra, and equivariant parameters are replaced by coweights of the Lie algebra. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality can be derived as a special case of the affine version. Finally, we examine the relationship between equivariant quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality and equivariant quantum group duality, showing that the former follows from the latter. This relationship also yields an alternative proof of equivariant quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality. Finally, the paper illustrates the SiD detector's capability to identify the Higgs boson decaying into a pair of electrons, a process that remains undetectable at the LHC. Amorphous ice is hypothesized to contain nanometer-scale regions of low-density amorphous (LDA) ice that are structurally distinct from the surrounding high-density amorphous (HDA) matrix. These LDA domains are believed to be responsible for the material's glassy behavior. This study investigates the structural characteristics of these potential LDA domains using molecular dynamics simulations. We examine the structural and thermodynamic properties of both HDA and LDA ices, as well as their interconversion, by analyzing the radial distribution function, orientational order parameter, and enthalpy. Our findings indicate that the amorphous ices generated in our simulations are structurally homogeneous, lacking any distinct domains. Furthermore, the transition between HDA and LDA ices is found to be continuous, with no evidence of a first-order phase transition. Consequently, our results suggest that the glassy nature of amorphous ice arises from its amorphous structure itself, rather than from the presence of separate LDA and HDA domains. This conclusion is supported by the observation that both HDA and LDA ices exhibit glassy properties. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the potential existence of superfluidity in amorphous ice. Our analysis indicates that while HDA ice is unlikely to be a superfluid, LDA ice may possess superfluid properties. This suggests that the superfluid nature of amorphous ice could stem from the superfluid characteristics of its LDA regions. Additionally, we examine the impact of pressure on the superfluid properties of LDA ice. Our results show that pressure can induce a first-order phase transition in LDA ice, transforming it into HDA ice, which would consequently eliminate its superfluid properties. This transition is consistent with experimental data. Overall, our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the structural and thermodynamic properties of amorphous ice, as well as its potential superfluid nature. These insights are crucial for advancing our knowledge of this unique material and its applications in various fields. Our research underscores the significance of amorphous ice in scientific inquiry and its potential to drive future technological advancements. By elucidating the fundamental properties of amorphous ice, our work paves the way for new discoveries and innovations in this fascinating field. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper comprehension of the complex behavior of water and its various phases, which is essential for a wide range of scientific and technological applications. Our study highlights the critical role of amorphous ice in advancing our understanding of this enigmatic material and its potential to inspire future breakthroughs

This study presents high-resolution Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy (STM) images of graphite, gold, and silicon surfaces, accompanied by a detailed analysis of their atomic structures. By employing constant height and constant current scanning modes, we successfully resolved the lattice structures of all three materials. Furthermore, we calculated the local density of features (LDF) for each surface using a 3x3 pixel sliding window. The results indicate that the LDF values for gold and silicon are nearly identical, whereas graphite exhibits a significantly lower LDF. These findings are supported by the respective atomic spacings: 0.246 nm for graphite, 0.408 nm for gold, and 0.384 nm for silicon. Additionally, we observed that the LDF values for gold and silicon remain relatively uniform across the scanned areas, while graphite displays greater variability. This variation in graphite is attributed to its anisotropic nature, which causes the STM tip to interact differently with the atomic rows oriented along the x and y axes. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for future STM applications. The accompanying dataset includes 3x3 pixel images of the three materials, along with their corresponding LDF maps and associated metadata. This data can facilitate further research into surface properties and atomic structures, as well as support the development of new STM techniques and algorithms. The dataset is accessible via the following link: https://github.com/abdullahkhan12345/STM-Atomic-Resolution-Imaging-and-Measurement-of-the-Local-Density-of-Features-of-Graphite-Gold-and-Silicon-using-Scanning-Tunnelling-Microscopy. We encourage researchers to utilize this data to advance their work in surface science and nanotechnology. The source code used to generate the LDF maps is also available at: https://github.com/abdullahkhan12345/STM-Atomic-Resolution-Imaging-and-Measurement-of-the-Local-Density-of-Features-of-Graphite-Gold-and-Silicon-using-Scanning-Tunnelling-Microscopy. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs (Isabelle AFP) is a widely utilized repository for verified theorems, with its contents increasingly employed in theorem proving research. However, the diverse origins of its contributions have resulted in significant inconsistencies in the quality of proof documents, hindering researchers from efficiently locating and utilizing relevant results. This paper introduces a framework designed to analyze and enhance the AFP, enabling the efficient identification of formalized theorems and their application in new proofs. The framework comprises two primary components: a data analysis module that examines the repository's structure and content, and a theorem recommendation module that suggests appropriate theorems to assist users during proof construction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework can effectively identify relevant theorems and aid users in completing proofs. Furthermore, the framework's integration into the AFP has yielded substantial improvements in the archive's quality. Ultra-low-frequency (ULF) waves within the magnetosphere are typically visualized through spectrograms, which plot signal intensity against time and frequency. However, these waves can also be rendered as audio, offering a complementary method for human data analysis. This study investigates the optimal approach for making ULF waves audible. We demonstrate that the most effective strategy involves a linear mapping of frequency to pitch, combined with a logarithmic mapping of wave amplitude to volume. Furthermore, we show that the magnetosphere's dynamic nature allows for the creation of both real-time and near real-time ULF wave audio. Finally, we illustrate the value of auditory analysis by presenting an example of how listening to ULF waves can reveal patterns that remain obscured in spectrograms. These findings establish a robust framework for future research into the audibility of ULF waves. The associated Python code is accessible at https://github.com/ulf-audio. Additionally, ULF wave audio files from the OMNIWeb and the University of Colorado Boulder's Space Environment Center are available at https://github.com/ulf-audio/ulf-audio-data. This study examines the thermodynamic characteristics of charged, rotating dilaton black holes interacting with logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics. The analysis covers the calculation of the metric, horizon radius, temperature, entropy, electric potential, and angular velocity. Furthermore, the paper explores the impact of the nonlinear parameter on the system's thermodynamic behavior. Finally, the first law of thermodynamics and the Smarr formula are derived and discussed. The findings indicate that the nonlinear parameter influences the horizon radius, temperature, entropy, electric potential, and angular velocity, while the dilaton parameter affects the horizon radius and temperature. Additionally, the study confirms that these black hole solutions satisfy the first law of thermodynamics and the Smarr formula. Finally, the Hawking temperature is computed, and the conditions for the existence of an inner and outer horizon are established. Finally, the phase transition is analyzed, revealing that the system undergoes a second-order phase transition. The critical point is determined as $r_{cr}=1.

This paper introduces a text memory structure designed to store and retrieve text data using a memory-based approach. The authors argue that current text representations are inadequate for supporting text-based machine learning, as they fail to capture the full complexity of text. To address this, the proposed structure enables the storage of text data in a memory-based framework. The authors contend that this structure is essential for advancing text-based machine learning, particularly for tasks involving text similarity and retrieval. The paper details the structure's design and implementation, demonstrating its effectiveness through experiments on text similarity and retrieval tasks. The results indicate that the structure successfully stores and retrieves text data, thereby supporting machine learning applications in these domains. Furthermore, the structure is shown to be scalable, capable of handling large volumes of text data. The paper establishes that CCR algebras and CAR algebras are connected through a continuous sequence of Cuntz-Toeplitz algebras, with the endpoints being the CAR and CCR algebras, respectively. This sequence is parameterized by a value in the interval [0,1], where 0 corresponds to the CAR algebra and 1 corresponds to the CCR algebra. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that every irreducible representation of the CCR algebra is unitarily equivalent to the Fock representation, and they provide an explicit formula for the isomorphism between the CCR algebra and the CAR algebra. Additionally, the study examines the relationship between the symplectic form and the parameter of the Cuntz-Toeplitz algebra. Finally, the authors prove that the CCR algebra is isomorphic to the inductive limit of the CAR algebra and the C*-algebra generated by the Toeplitz operators T_{e^{it}} and T_{e^{it}}*. The paper concludes by presenting an open question. Keywords: CCR algebra, CAR algebra, Cuntz-Toeplitz algebra, symplectic form. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 46L40, 46L52, 46L55. The TW Hydrae association, a nearby star-forming region, is currently the subject of intense observational scrutiny. This study aims to forecast the radio signatures of two competing disk evolution models—photoevaporation and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) winds—by analyzing the future observational capabilities of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA). We utilized a radiative transfer code to simulate radio emission from disks around TW Hydrae-class stars, incorporating both photoevaporation and MHD wind models. Our results indicate that the photoevaporation model predicts a radio flux of approximately 100 microJy at 1.3 cm, whereas the MHD wind model predicts a significantly lower flux of about 1 microJy. These predictions suggest that the SKA will be capable of detecting radio emission from TW Hydrae disks, thereby offering a means to distinguish between these competing models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the MHD wind model can be tested by observing the radio emission from the ionized gas within the disk's outer regions. This approach could provide critical insights into the mechanisms driving the formation of low-mass stars and planetary systems. Ultimately, our findings underscore the SKA's potential to advance our understanding of the processes governing star and planet formation. Additionally, we highlight the necessity of developing a comprehensive model that integrates both photoevaporation and MHD wind effects to accurately describe the evolution of protoplanetary disks. We demonstrate that for any integer $n \geq 2$, there exists a group with rank $n$ exhibiting near-exponential remainder finiteness growth. This finding contrasts with the observation that groups of rank $n$ typically display only polynomial growth in terms of their number of remainders. Furthermore, we establish that groups with rank $n$ and finite cohomological dimension possess at most exponential growth for their number of remainders. Additionally, we provide an explicit upper bound on the growth of remainders for groups of rank $n$ within a broad class of solvable groups. Finally, we present a significant extension of our primary result to residually finite groups. Our findings are derived from an analysis of the relationship between the growth of remainders and the growth of maximal subgroups. We also introduce a novel method for estimating the growth of maximal subgroups in various group classes, which may have independent applications. Specifically, we prove that for any $n \geq 2$, the number of conjugacy classes of maximal subgroups of rank $n$ in the free solvable group of rank $n$ and derived length $k$ grows exponentially with $k$. This result is achieved by reducing the problem to the study of free subgroups of finite index within the group. We anticipate that this approach will be applicable to other groups of solvable type. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews fundamental definitions and concepts; Section 3 examines the relationship between maximal subgroup growth and remainder growth; Section 4 addresses the growth of maximal subgroups in free solvable groups; and Section 5 constructs groups with near-exponential growth for their number of remainders. The final section generalizes this construction to residually finite groups. The Appendix contains a detailed proof of a theorem regarding the growth of maximal subgroups in free solvable groups, which was omitted from the original publication. This proof relies on the work of B. B. Newman and C. C. Sims, who established that the number of conjugacy classes of subgroups of rank $n$ in the free group of rank $n$ grows exponentially with $n$. We also include a brief discussion on the relationship between this theorem and the growth of maximal subgroups in free solvable groups. This study examines the stability of a damped extended Euler-Bernoulli beam governed by a fourth-order equation, where the beam is supported by a nonlinear foundation. The foundation's nonlinearity is modeled using a continuous function that satisfies specific growth and sign conditions. We establish the asymptotic stability of the system through a combination of energy methods and frequency analysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the decay rate of the system's energy is directly proportional to the growth rate of the foundation's nonlinearity. Finally, we confirm the optimality of this result by constructing a specific nonlinear system that achieves the same growth rate for its nonlinearity. Additionally, we derive a nonlinear beam equation by applying a change of variables to the extended Euler-Bernoulli beam system. We introduce a machine learning approach to predict nuclear masses, utilizing a physics-informed graph neural network (GNN) trained on a dataset combining experimental data with masses derived from various theoretical models. This architecture incorporates a graph representation of nuclei and is guided by the fundamental principles of nuclear physics. Our results demonstrate that the GNN surpasses both the experimental dataset and other models, achieving a root mean square deviation of 0.45 MeV for masses below the drip line. This level of precision is essential for $r$-process studies, where accurate masses are critical for determining nuclear reaction rates. Furthermore, we extend the training to the neutron-rich region to support $r$-process investigations, achieving a root mean square deviation of 0.6 MeV for masses exceeding the drip line. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of the model's performance across different mass regions and its ability to extrapolate into unexplored areas. Finally, we apply the GNN to predict fission fragment masses, a key component in $r$-process modeling. The GNN successfully predicts fission fragment masses with a root mean square deviation of 0.6 MeV, a figure comparable to the uncertainty in the input masses. These findings indicate that the GNN is a valuable tool for advancing $r$-process research. The code is accessible at https://github.com/astroML/nuclear-masses. Sapphire serves as a leading substrate for superconducting quantum circuits, with its microwave dielectric loss tangent ($\tan\delta$) being a critical parameter for assessing its impact on quantum system performance. This study presents a precise measurement of $\tan\delta$ for high-purity sapphire at cryogenic temperatures, achieving a sensitivity of 1 part per billion (ppb). We demonstrate that $\tan\delta$ is directly proportional to the microwave photon occupation number, confirming that thermal phonons are the primary source of dielectric loss. Furthermore, we establish a quantitative relationship between $\tan\delta$ and the material's impurity concentration, revealing that the thermal phonon-induced loss is approximately 100 times greater than the loss caused by trace impurities. These findings provide a robust framework for evaluating sapphire quality and predicting its dielectric loss contributions in quantum technologies. Additionally, we report a record-breaking quality factor of $Q=1.5\times10^{10}$ for a high-purity sapphire resonator at 4.2 K, a value that exceeds the theoretical limit for sapphire substrates. These results underscore the necessity for further advancements in sapphire purification techniques to meet the stringent requirements of quantum applications. This paper introduces H4M, a heterogeneous, multi-source, multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-distributed dataset designed for socioeconomic analytics in Beijing. The dataset comprises four distinct data sources: (1) a street-level map of Beijing, (2) a collection of 100,000 user-generated reviews from Dianping.com, (3) 100,000 check-in records from Dianping.com, and (4) 100,000 reviews from Maoyan.com. These sources are distributed across four servers, each hosting one source. The data is segmented into 100,000 user profiles, where each profile contains four views corresponding to the four sources. This study presents the dataset and its applications, demonstrating its utility in three key areas: (1) multi-view multi-modal multi-source heterogeneous data fusion for socioeconomic analytics, (2) multi-view multi-modal multi-source heterogeneous data fusion for user profiling, and (3) multi-view multi-modal multi-source heterogeneous data fusion for Beijing tourism analytics. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a leading approach for learning from graph-structured data, demonstrating strong performance across various domains. However, training GNNs from scratch is often costly and time-consuming, especially when data is scarce. Transfer learning offers a solution by enabling the reuse of knowledge gained from previous tasks to accelerate the training of new ones. This paper provides a comprehensive review of transfer learning within the GNN domain, examining its applications, methods, and challenges. We begin by defining transfer learning and its relevance to GNNs, followed by an analysis of its use cases and the specific techniques employed. Finally, we discuss the current state of the field and outline potential future research directions. Our goal is to offer a thorough overview of transfer learning for GNNs, highlighting both its opportunities and obstacles. This paper introduces a recommender system grounded in a dual feature allocation model. The process begins by learning feature allocation models for both users and items, where features represent the latent interests of users and latent attributes of items. Subsequently, a dual feature allocation model is established to identify the most relevant user-feature-item triplets. Finally, recommendations are generated by ranking items based on the relevance scores derived from these triplets. Experimental results demonstrate that the system's performance is comparable to or exceeds that of state-of-the-art methods. We demonstrate that for any universe of size $u$, a set system with set size $k$, and $\epsilon < 1/k$, there exists a coloring of the universe using $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}k)$ colors such that every pair of sets differing by at least $\epsilon u$ receives distinct colors. This result provides an upper bound on the set separation number, a parameter with applications in data streams and property testing. Our approach is straightforward and relies on a novel application of the regularity lemma. Furthermore, we establish that our bound is nearly tight for data stream applications, improving upon the previous best upper bound of $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}u)$. We also present a variant applicable to data streams where the set size $k$ is unknown, requiring only $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2}\sqrt{u})$ space. Additionally, we prove that for any universe of size $u$ and set size $k$, there exists a set system where every pair of sets differs by at least $\Omega(1/\sqrt{k})$ elements, thereby showing that our data stream bound is tight up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we derive a set separation bound for set systems with bounded set intersection, which is tight up to logarithmic factors. Our primary method involves a new, simple, and efficient algorithm for the densest $k$-subgraph problem, which we believe has independent significance. This algorithm achieves a runtime of $2^{O(\sqrt{k})}n^{O(1)}$ and a multiplicative approximation factor of $O(\sqrt{k})$, surpassing the best prior runtime of $2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}$ with a factor of $O(k)$. Our algorithm is based on a new rounding technique for semidefinite programming relaxations of densest $k$-subgraph. We also present a variant of this algorithm that runs in $2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}$ time and achieves a $1+\epsilon$ approximation for densest $k$-subgraph when the number of edges is at least $\Omega(k^2\log^2 n)$. We demonstrate that the non-analytic momentum dependence of the Pauli spin susceptibility in Heisenberg magnets, which arises from the Fermi surface of magnons, significantly influences the critical exponents. Specifically, the exponent $\delta$ is calculated as $\delta=15/4$ for the three-dimensional (3D) magnon gas and $\delta=7/3$ for the two-dimensional (2D) magnon gas. These theoretical findings align with the exponents derived from the renormalization group method. Additionally, we show that the magnon gas model accurately describes the temperature dependence of the spin susceptibility in the paramagnetic phase of real materials, including $^{3}$He magnets and certain 3D Heisenberg antiferromagnets. The calculated values for the critical exponents $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are $\beta=1/4$ and $\gamma=1/2$, respectively, which match the experimental data. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the critical behavior of other quantum many-body systems. We introduce an on-chip optical system designed to trap, manipulate, and read out a single atom using a multi-grating architecture. This setup generates three distinct optical trapping potentials and a Raman transition beam from a single laser source. The optical trap is engineered to capture the atom at a specific location within the chip, while the Raman transition beam facilitates the manipulation of the atom's internal state. Subsequently, a fluorescence readout beam illuminates the atom to detect its state. This multi-grating design offers a compact, integrated solution for single-atom manipulation, paving the way for the development of quantum information processors. Experimental results confirm the successful trapping and manipulation of a single atom, with an average trap lifetime exceeding 10 seconds and a Raman transition probability greater than 90%. Furthermore, the integrated system achieves a single-atom readout fidelity of 99.5%. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed multi-grating architecture for integrated single-atom manipulation. The entire system is fabricated on a silicon nitride chip with a footprint of only 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm. This work was published in *Optics Express* (2021, Vol. 29, No. 12, pp. 18330-18340). This study investigates the linear and nonlinear Hall conductance in two-dimensional interacting electron systems featuring disorder. We demonstrate that the nonlinear Hall conductance scales linearly with the electric field, a finding that remains valid even when the system is in a metallic state. Furthermore, we show that interaction effects can be eliminated through a transformation of the electron operators. Finally, we establish that the nonlinear Hall conductance is governed by the second moment of the Berry curvature distribution. Additionally, we confirm that the interaction-induced correction to the linear Hall conductance is negligible compared to the nonlinear contribution. These results are derived using a combination of perturbation theory and the self-consistent Born approximation. Our findings indicate that the nonlinear Hall effect is robust against interactions and can be observed in metallic systems. This conclusion is supported by numerical simulations of a two-dimensional square lattice model incorporating both spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions. The simulations reveal that the nonlinear Hall conductance is directly proportional to the second moment of the Berry curvature distribution. These outcomes suggest that the nonlinear Hall effect may be detectable in various materials, including those with metallic characteristics. This research expands upon our earlier work [Phys. Rev. B 105, 045115 (2022)] by extending the analysis to interacting systems. Our findings offer new avenues for investigating the nonlinear Hall effect in materials where interactions play a significant role. The methodology employed in this study can be applied to a broad spectrum of materials, ranging from topological insulators to strongly correlated systems. Ultimately, this work underscores the potential of the nonlinear Hall effect as a valuable tool for characterizing materials and their electronic properties. By elucidating the impact of interactions on the nonlinear Hall effect, this research paves the way for future studies on this phenomenon in materials with complex electronic structures. This paper introduces a novel direct transcription approach designed to optimize dynamic systems with mixed-integer constraints. The method iteratively refines Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) approximations of the original problem, utilizing a user-defined terminal time to generate a feasible solution. This strategy is demonstrated through the optimization of a dual-patient ventilator, a device capable of supporting two individuals simultaneously. The ventilator's design aims to reduce the risk of viral transmission by preventing exhaled air from one patient from reaching the other. The study evaluates the direct transcription method against the standard Multiple Shooting method, which relies on iterative linearization. Results indicate that the direct transcription approach achieves superior convergence rates and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the optimized ventilator design demonstrates significant potential for mitigating viral spread. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions. We demonstrate that for a bicritical rational map $f$ of degree $d\ge 2$, the deck clusters of the iterates $f^n$ are situated within the Julia set of $f$. Furthermore, if $f$ is not conjugate to a Lattès map, these clusters constitute the entirety of the Julia set. This result extends the findings of Buff and Chéritat regarding bicritical polynomials. Additionally, we establish that the deck clusters of $f^n$ are precisely the points where $f$ fails to be injective on the level sets of $f^{n-1}$. As an application, we confirm that the deck clusters of $f^n$ remain bounded whenever $f$ is post-critically finite. Finally, we provide examples of bicritical rational maps where the deck clusters of the iterates do not form the complete Julia set. These examples include Lattès maps and maps possessing Siegel disks, with the latter being constructed based on a recent discovery by J. D. Hill regarding Siegel disks in rational maps. The paper also incorporates an appendix by J. D. Hill, which offers an alternative characterization of Siegel disks in rational maps. The electronic characteristics of monolayer and few-layer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are highly sensitive to their structural parameters. This study employs density functional theory (DFT) and the GW approximation to analyze the thickness-dependent variations in work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity for MoS₂, MoSe₂, WS₂, and WSe₂. Our findings indicate that GW calculations yield superior accuracy in predicting these properties compared to DFT. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that both the band gap and the work function of these TMDs vary with thickness. Specifically, the work function increases as the number of layers grows, with the most pronounced changes occurring during the transition from monolayer to bilayer. Finally, we compare the calculated work functions with experimental data to validate our theoretical approach. These insights are essential for the design and fabrication of next-generation electronic and optoelectronic devices. Additionally, the GW method utilized in this work is applicable to other materials, including graphene, carbon nanotubes, and transition metal dichalcogenides. This study examines the efficiency of the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method in reaching steady-state solutions for rarefied gas flows. We introduce a novel approach to evaluate the convergence of DSMC simulations, utilizing a metric that quantifies the statistical uncertainty of Monte Carlo estimators. This metric is derived from the sample variance of the estimators and their associated Monte Carlo sample sizes. Our findings indicate that the proposed metric effectively identifies the steady state of DSMC simulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the DSMC algorithm can achieve a steady state within dozens of iterations when employing a dynamic time step. These results are illustrated through two-dimensional simulations of a rarefied gas stream. The proposed metric is applicable to any DSMC simulation, regardless of the specific flow conditions. Additionally, the method is versatile and can be utilized for other Monte Carlo simulations. These findings suggest that the events may originate from a non-conventional source, such as axion particle nuggets. This paper explores the potential for axion nuggets to produce such a cluster and examines the implications of these results for axion physics. We introduce a novel statistical mechanical framework for analyzing two-dimensional Pauli lattices, which are defined by their initial Hadamard state and subsequent random Pauli measurements. This approach enables the calculation of the probability distribution for the count of +1 measurement outcomes across all possible measurement sequences. Furthermore, we establish a link between these 2D Pauli lattices and one-dimensional Pauli chains, thereby extending the latter's established connection to the Ising model. Leveraging this framework, we derive a comprehensive set of identities regarding random Pauli measurements on graph states, including a specific identity that facilitates the computation of these probability distributions. Finally, we present a general method for calculating these distributions for any graph state constructed via the method of local complementation. We introduce a novel class of magnetic Bloch states within twisted bilayer graphene subjected to a $2\pi$ flux per unit cell and a perpendicular magnetic field. This proposal is supported by a theoretical analysis of the energy gap between the flat band and the first excited band, which indicates that the system remains in the ground state throughout the flux variation. These results suggest that the $2\pi$ flux states can be prepared without inducing Landau level transitions. Our findings provide a comprehensive theoretical framework for interpreting the anomalous Hall effect and flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at $2\pi$ flux. Furthermore, our proposed method for preparing $2\pi$ flux states may facilitate the creation of new quantum materials. The Kitaev model, originally formulated for spin-1/2 systems, has recently been realized in Kitaev materials such as $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ and $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$. Furthermore, we observed that the Kitaev interaction in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ increases with pressure, suggesting that the Kitaev interaction in this material is tunable. These findings offer new insights into the interplay between Kitaev interactions and dimerization in Kitaev materials. Additionally, the pressure-induced dimerization in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ may facilitate the emergence of Kitaev quantum spin liquid phases. Synthetic control methods are widely used to estimate causal effects by creating a weighted combination of control units that approximates the treated unit's pre-intervention characteristics. This paper presents a theoretical framework to guide the application of synthetic controls in causal inference. We demonstrate that the method achieves consistency when the treated unit is a weighted average of the control units, a condition we term "local linearity." Furthermore, we establish that the synthetic control estimator possesses the Neyman orthogonality property, ensuring robustness against overfitting. This property enables the development of a debiased estimator that remains consistent even when local linearity is only approximately valid. Additionally, we prove that the synthetic control estimator is root-n consistent and asymptotically normal under the local linearity assumption, provided the number of control units increases at a sufficient rate. These findings offer a comprehensive theoretical basis for utilizing synthetic controls in causal inference. The paper also includes a simulation study to evaluate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators. Finally, we apply the synthetic control estimator to analyze the impact of the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA) on welfare receipt rates. Our results indicate that the synthetic control estimator yields more accurate inferences than the standard synthetic control approach. The PRWORA analysis reveals that the reform reduced welfare receipt rates by approximately 10% to 15% in the treated states. This study introduces a privacy-preserving framework for computing the Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance between two graphs. The proposed method ensures differential privacy (DP) during the sampling phase, which is essential for maintaining privacy in graph-based learning tasks. We demonstrate that the $L_2$ error of the empirical GW distance converges to the true GW distance at a rate of $O(n^{-1/2})$, where $n$ represents the number of nodes. Furthermore, we establish that the $L_2$ error of the empirical DP GW distance also converges to the true GW distance at the same rate. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical experiments. These results indicate that the empirical GW distance calculated via our method remains close to the true GW distance, even under conditions of differential privacy. Additionally, we observe that the empirical DP GW distance is highly sensitive to the privacy budget $\epsilon$, with a lower $\epsilon$ value leading to a greater deviation from the true GW distance. This deviation is particularly pronounced when the number of nodes is small. However, as the number of nodes increases, the impact of the privacy budget diminishes, and the empirical DP GW distance becomes increasingly accurate. These findings underscore the critical role of the privacy budget in the proposed framework. Overall, our method offers a promising solution for privacy-preserving GW distance computation, with potential applications in graph-based learning and other related fields. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2020/GWDP}.

Keywords: Gromov-Wasserstein distance, Local differential privacy, Graph representation learning, Graph neural networks.

We present revised and novel constraints on neutrinoless double beta decay and dark matter interactions involving platinum isotopes $^{190}$Pt and $^{194}$Pt. These limits are derived from the absence of observed events in the GERDA experiment, which utilized $^{76}$Ge detectors. Our analysis incorporates state-of-the-art nuclear matrix element calculations and employs a state-of-the-art framework for dark matter-induced processes. The resulting limits on neutrino mass are competitive with other isotopes, while the constraints on dark matter-induced processes represent the most stringent limits available to date. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sensitivity of $^{190}$Pt and $^{194}$Pt to dark matter is comparable to that of $^{136}$Xe, a widely used isotope in current and upcoming direct detection experiments. Consequently, our findings underscore the potential of platinum as a promising candidate for future neutrinoless double beta decay experiments and for advancing the search for dark matter. This study also offers a comprehensive overview of the nuclear physics and experimental requirements necessary for such investigations. Additionally, we provide a detailed discussion of the challenges associated with the production and purification of high-purity platinum. Finally, we outline the prospects for a dedicated platinum experiment, including a preliminary assessment of the feasibility of producing a 100 kg source of high-purity platinum. This study examines the generalized three-dimensional Ermakov system, which is defined by three coupled second-order ordinary differential equations. The analysis demonstrates that this system retains the full $SO(3)$ symmetry of the standard three-dimensional harmonic oscillator. Furthermore, it establishes that the system admits two additional independent first integrals, thereby ensuring complete integrability. These preservation laws are expressed as the product of the first integrals of the equations of motion and the third integral derived from the Lagrange identity. The paper also explores the connection between these findings and the existence of a non-local symmetry within the generalized Ermakov system. Finally, the results are extended to the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system. In this broader context, the preservation laws are formulated as the product of the first integrals of the equations of motion and the integral obtained from the Lagrange identity. Additionally, the existence of a non-local symmetry in the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system is confirmed. This work is motivated by the need to investigate the existence of non-local symmetries in nonlinear systems, a topic of significant interest in both mathematical and physical research. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results. Keywords: Generalized $n$-dimensional harmonic oscillator; Generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system; Lagrange identity; Non-local symmetry; Preservation laws. This paper presents a characterization of semi-transitive split graphs, which extends the findings of Neumann and Trotter (2002) regarding chordal graphs. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the minimum number of edges in a semi-transitive split graph with $n$ vertices is $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + n - 1$. This result contrasts with the case for chordal split graphs, where the minimum edge count is $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + n - 2$. The paper also examines the maximum number of edges in such graphs, revealing that semi-transitive split graphs can possess more edges than their chordal counterparts. Furthermore, the study identifies a class of semi-transitive split graphs that are not chordal, thereby confirming that the class of semi-transitive split graphs is distinct from that of chordal split graphs. Finally, the paper establishes that the maximum number of edges in a semi-transitive split graph is $\lfloor n^2/2 \rfloor$. This finding is consistent with the known result for chordal split graphs, which also have a maximum edge count of $\lfloor n^2/2 \rfloor$. The authors conjecture that semi-transitive split graphs are precisely those split graphs that contain no semi-transitive subgraph of order $n$. This conjecture aligns with the broader conjecture that semi-transitive graphs are exactly those graphs devoid of semi-transitive subgraphs of order $n$. Additionally, the paper provides a characterization of semi-transitive split graphs that are not claw-free, contrasting this with the fact that all chordal split graphs are claw-free. This study introduces a deep neural network designed to identify tau leptons undergoing hadronic decays. The network utilizes kinematic and particle flow variables to differentiate tau decays from background processes, including jets originating from quarks and gluons, as well as hadronic decays of other leptons. This study examines intermodal forward Brillouin scattering within a solid-core photonic lattice fiber, which is engineered to confine light in a flat-top intensity profile. The fiber's periodic microstructure creates a photonic bandgap that blocks most higher-order modes, thereby suppressing intermodal scattering. However, we identify specific higher-order modes that fall within the bandgap and exhibit strong Brillouin coupling with the fundamental mode. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the coupling coefficients for these modes can be adjusted by modifying the microstructure's geometry. These findings offer a pathway to achieve multi-frequency operation in photonic lattice fibers. Additionally, we show that the proposed method can be applied to other photonic lattice fibers, enabling the selection of higher-order modes that are otherwise difficult to excite. Finally, we explore the potential for utilizing these modes in solid-core photonic lattice fibers for applications such as sensing and optical communications. This study examines the electromagnetic interaction between an electron or positron and a dense nucleus during ultra-peripheral ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, the electromagnetic field generated by the electron or positron exerts a significant influence on the photon flux emitted by the dense nucleus. Additionally, the photon flux resulting from the electromagnetic interaction between the electron or positron and the nucleus is found to be substantially higher than the photon flux produced by the dense nucleus alone. These findings indicate that the electromagnetic interaction between low transverse momentum electrons or positrons and dense nuclei plays a crucial role in ultra-peripheral ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Consequently, this interaction must be accounted for when analyzing the production of low transverse momentum electrons and positrons in such collisions. Ultimately, the study seeks to contribute to a deeper understanding of the electromagnetic interaction between low transverse momentum electrons and positrons with dense nuclei in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The findings may also assist in the design of future experiments investigating this phenomenon. Finally, the results could contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the electromagnetic interaction between low transverse momentum electrons and positrons with dense nuclei in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The outcomes of this research may also aid in the development of new experimental methods for studying this interaction. This paper introduces a motion planning framework utilizing Control Barrier Functions (CBF) to ensure secure motion for dynamic robots within time-varying environments. The proposed CBF constraints are designed to be robust against model uncertainties and external disturbances, thereby guaranteeing collision-free trajectories. To address the resulting constrained optimal control problem, we develop a model predictive control (MPC) strategy that incorporates a novel cost function. This cost function ensures that the robot reaches its target while maintaining a safe distance from obstacles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed MPC scheme ensures recursive feasibility and ultimately drives the robot to the desired destination. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through simulation experiments. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the computational complexity of the CBF constraints and the associated optimization problem. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future research directions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/CBF-MPC.

For a ring $R$, let $\mathcal{I}(R)$ represent the collection of all its ideals. The enveloping number of $R$, denoted as $\mathcal{E}(R)$, is defined as the count of distinct rings that can be formed by selecting two ideals $I$ and $J$ from $\mathcal{I}(R)$ such that their product $I \cdot J$ equals zero. This paper investigates various properties of this enveloping number. Specifically, for any commutative ring $R$ with unity, we establish the inequality $\mathcal{E}(R) \leqslant 2^{2\omega(R)}$, where $\omega(R)$ signifies the maximum number of pairwise comaximal ideals in $R$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bound is sharp. Additionally, we examine the enveloping numbers for specific rings, including those of integers modulo $n$, Boolean rings, and rings of continuous real-valued functions. Finally, we explore the relationship between the enveloping number and the Jacobson radical of a ring. As an application, we derive an upper limit for the enveloping number of a commutative ring $R$ with unity, expressed in terms of the number of maximal ideals in $R/\mathcal{N}(R)$, where $\mathcal{N}(R)$ denotes the nilradical of $R$. This limit is proven to be sharp. Notably, this result indicates that the upper bound for $\mathcal{E}(R)$ is independent of the Jacobson radical of $R$. Consequently, we establish that $\mathcal{E}(R) \leqslant 2^{2\omega(R/J(R))}$, where $J(R)$ is the Jacobson radical of $R$. This inequality is also shown to be sharp. Finally, we provide an example of a commutative ring $R$ with unity for which $\mathcal{E}(R) = 2^{2\omega(R/J(R))}$. This example confirms that the bound is attained and illustrates that the enveloping number of $R$ does not depend on the nilpotency index of its Jacobson radical. In conclusion, we propose an open question regarding the determination of the precise value of $\mathcal{E}(R)$ for a commutative ring $R$ with unity. Additionally, we define the enveloping spectrum of $R$ as the set of all possible enveloping numbers for its quotient rings.

We introduce a novel class of links, termed horizon saddle links, which emerge from the monodromy of affine holomorphic dilations defined on open Riemann surfaces with specific punctures. These links exhibit numerous remarkable characteristics, including the presence of open book decompositions, torus satellite structures, and the ability to be realized as 2-bridge links. Furthermore, we establish that the Reeb flow associated with any such link is topologically equivalent to the Reeb flow of a torus knot. Additionally, we demonstrate that every dilation surface possesses a unique invariant dilation foliation, and the leaves of this foliation are precisely the horizons of the corresponding horizon saddle links. Finally, we prove that the Reeb flow of a dilation surface is Morse-Smale if and only if its associated foliation is trivial. This result provides a characterization of dilation surfaces with Morse-Smale dynamics in terms of their leaves. As a consequence, we derive an explicit formula for the number of dilation surfaces with Morse-Smale dynamics within any fixed stratum. The methodology employed relies on the analysis of the Reeb flow on the unit tangent bundle of the dilation surface. This approach also yields an alternative proof of the result by Lanneau and Thurston regarding the finiteness of strata containing Morse-Smale dilation surfaces. The paper concludes with several open questions. This paper investigates the conditional distribution of a Gaussian process given a specific realization of another Gaussian process. Furthermore, we propose a method to construct a version of the conditional distribution that is consistent across all time points. The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a comprehensive neutrino research initiative designed to advance our understanding of fundamental particle physics, astrophysics, and cosmology. As a global collaboration, it involves over 3,000 scientists from 36 nations. The project's centerpiece is a 700-kiloton liquid argon time projection chamber situated 1.5 kilometers underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, USA. This detector will be supplied with a high-intensity neutrino beam generated at Fermilab in Illinois, USA, utilizing a proton beam of up to 120 kW. The experiment aims to precisely measure neutrino oscillation parameters, investigate the neutrino mass hierarchy, and determine the neutrino CP phase. Additionally, DUNE will conduct searches for sterile neutrinos, provide the first observations of supernova neutrinos, and analyze neutrinos from the Sun, Earth, and atmospheric sources. This paper outlines the experimental design and current status of DUNE. It also presents a preliminary assessment of the experiment's sensitivity regarding the neutrino mass hierarchy and CP violation, alongside a discussion on the potential for discovering sterile neutrinos. Finally, the paper addresses the ongoing construction and operational timeline of the project. The DUNE collaboration anticipates the start of data collection in 2027. For further information, visit the official website at http://www.dunescience.org. This paper introduces the VO (Value Object) concept, which represents a class possessing a well-defined, advanced semantics. We provide a definition of VOs grounded in first-order logic and demonstrate how to model VO refinement and related constructs within the Z notation. Furthermore, we establish several properties of VOs and their refinements, including the preservation of VOs during refinement. Finally, we illustrate the application of this VO-based methodology within the Open-Source Software tool, ZNoter. The tool enables the formalization of VOs and VO refinement within the Z notation framework. Additionally, it supports the verification of the properties discussed in this paper. The tool is available at: https://github.com/vo-refinement/ZNoter.

The VO concept is particularly valuable for managing complex objects with rich semantics, such as those found in the domains of medicine and biology. In these fields, objects often possess intricate meanings that are difficult to capture using standard object-oriented programming techniques. The VO approach offers a solution by providing a formal method to define and reason about such complex objects.

The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 defines VOs; Section 4 addresses VO refinement; Section 5 presents properties of VOs and VO refinement; and Section 6 describes the VO formalization tool.

Replay buffers are a fundamental component of modern reinforcement learning, serving as a mechanism to mitigate data inefficiency by enabling agents to learn from past experiences. This paper introduces a novel replay buffer designed to enhance the sample efficiency of policy gradient methods. The proposed approach, termed Variance Diminution based Experience Replay (VDE), aims to reduce the variance of the policy gradient estimator. We demonstrate that VDE achieves this by prioritizing transitions with low variance, thereby improving the quality of the data utilized for policy updates. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the impact of VDE on the convergence of policy optimization algorithms. Experimental results confirm that VDE significantly boosts sample efficiency, delivering performance comparable to or superior to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we show that VDE enhances the stability of policy optimization, resulting in more consistent performance across multiple runs. The superbosonization equation and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation are two distinct approaches for extending bosonization to the realm of fermionic systems. This paper demonstrates that both methods yield equivalent results when applied to the one-dimensional Dirac fermion model. Furthermore, we establish a direct link between these techniques and show that the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation can be derived from the superbosonization equation. Finally, we apply these methods to the two-dimensional Dirac fermion model, revealing that the superbosonization approach fails in this context. Consequently, we introduce a novel generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation that successfully extends bosonization to fermionic systems in arbitrary dimensions. As an application, we utilize this new method to derive the exact partition function for the two-dimensional Dirac fermion model. Additionally, we demonstrate that the technique can be applied to the two-dimensional Thirring model, yielding a result consistent with existing literature. When creating a combined image from multiple observations, the resulting point spread function (PSF) is not merely a simple convolution of the individual PSFs. This discrepancy arises because the integration process involves weighting each observation, and these weights vary across the image. Consequently, the effective PSF of the final image is spatially dependent. This article outlines the derivation of this effective PSF and presents a method to estimate it. The approach is demonstrated using the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) and the James Webb Space Telescope's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam). The derived effective PSF is subsequently applied to a specific image combination to illustrate the phenomenon. The analysis reveals that the effective PSF is approximately 10% broader than the convolution of the individual PSFs, a factor that must be accounted for when performing photometry on the combined image. Furthermore, the study indicates that the effective PSF is not uniform across the entire image; instead, it varies with position, particularly near the edges of the observations. This spatial variation is most pronounced in the NIRCam image, where the PSF can be up to 20% broader at the image edges compared to the center. These findings are particularly significant for photometry conducted on the combined image. Finally, the paper provides a Python script to calculate the effective PSF for any given image combination. The code is available at https://github.com/jean-philippe-beaulieu/EffectivePSF. The script can be executed via the command line using the command: `python EffectivePSF.py --obs1 obs1.fits --obs2 obs2.fits --obs3 obs3.fits --weights weights.fits --output output.fits`. The required weights file can be generated using the `makeWeights.py` script, which is also included in the repository. The command to create the weights file is: `python makeWeights.py --obs1 obs1.fits --obs2 obs2.fits --obs3 obs3.fits --output weights.fits`. The `makeWeights.py` script is also accessible at https://github.com/jean-philippe-beaulieu/EffectivePSF. The example images used in this study are sourced from the Hubble Space Telescope's WFC3 and the James Webb Space Telescope's NIRCam. This study investigates the fracture strength of crystalline solids, with a specific focus on the influence of dislocations. We examine the fracture of a crystal containing a single edge dislocation subjected to uniaxial tension. By employing a continuum model, we demonstrate that the fracture strength is governed by the dislocation's core size, which is comparable to the interatomic spacing. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of dislocation interactions on fracture strength. Our findings indicate that the effect of dislocation-dislocation interactions is negligible when the dislocation density is low, whereas it becomes significant at high densities. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for polycrystalline materials. We investigate a random surface model defined by a Gaussian free field (GFF) interacting with $n$ multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions (SLEs), where the driving functions of these SLEs constitute a random log-gas. We demonstrate that the random surface defined by this model is equivalent to the Schramm-Werner random surface. Furthermore, we establish that the distribution of the random log-gas driving the multiple SLEs is equivalent to that of the Schramm-Werner random surface, and we determine the parameters of this log-gas. Finally, we prove that the correlation functions of the GFF coupled with $n$ SLEs can be expressed as the Schramm-Werner partition function. This work extends the findings of [Bertoin, Yau, and Zhang, 2021] regarding the CFT of the Schramm-Werner random surface. Additionally, we provide a novel proof of the conformal invariance of the Schramm-Werner random surface. The methodology employed in this paper is expected to be applicable to other random surface models. As an application, we derive the CFT of the GFF coupled with the CLE$_\kappa$-Coulomb gas random surface, which is relevant to the O(n) model. We introduce a straightforward classical verification protocol for quantum computations that utilizes quantum random access memory (QRAM). This approach extends the original classical verification method, which was limited to QRAM-free computations, by allowing the use of QRAM. The protocol maintains linear time complexity, matching the performance of the original method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the original classical verification scheme can be viewed as a specific instance of our generalized protocol. Consequently, our findings indicate that the traditional verification of quantum computations can be achieved in linear time. Additionally, we present a classical algorithm capable of generating valid witness states for the verification process in polynomial time. This algorithm is also applicable to the original classical verification scheme. Our results suggest that the traditional verification of quantum computations is feasible within linear time. Finally, we highlight that our proposed verification scheme is particularly well-suited for verifying the quantum advantage of the boson sampling experiment. Our method enables the verification of quantum advantage in boson sampling with a computational complexity of $O(n^3)$, where $n$ represents the number of modes. This represents a significant improvement over the $O(n^4)$ complexity of the original classical verification scheme. Therefore, our work demonstrates that the traditional verification of quantum computations can be accomplished in linear time. Stellar activity poses a significant challenge to the detection of exoplanet atmospheres, particularly at low spectral resolutions where the signal-to-noise ratio is low and the planet's spectral features are heavily blended. This study examines how stellar activity affects low-resolution transit spectroscopy and demonstrates that utilizing high-resolution data can mitigate these impacts. We analyzed the low-resolution transmission spectrum of the hot Jupiter WASP-12b, derived from high-resolution observations collected by the High Resolution Echelle Spectrometer (HiRes) on the Gemini North telescope. Our findings indicate that the low-resolution spectrum aligns well with a model incorporating a hydrogen-dominated atmosphere, a temperature of 1500 K, and a scale height of 1000 km. Furthermore, we show that high-resolution data enables the identification of activity-induced spectral features, thereby facilitating their removal from the low-resolution dataset. This approach offers a viable method for mitigating stellar activity in low-resolution transit spectra, provided that high-resolution observations are available. Consequently, this strategy could enhance the prospects for detecting exoplanet atmospheres using current and future low-resolution instruments. However, it is essential to note that this mitigation technique relies on the assumption that the high-resolution data is free from systematic errors. Finally, we demonstrate that the HiRes instrument can achieve the necessary level of precision to validate this approach. These results underscore the critical need for high-resolution observations to characterize stellar activity and establish a baseline for future low-resolution transit spectroscopy. Additionally, they highlight the importance of developing high-resolution instruments capable of observing exoplanets with sufficient precision to enable the mitigation of stellar activity. Such instruments will be vital for future exoplanet atmospheric studies. This work was conducted within the Gemini Observatory's Exoplanet Atmospheres Science Program. This study examines the swimming mechanics of the aquatic centipede *Trigoniulus geayi* by analyzing its kinematics, hydrodynamics, and energetics. We demonstrate that these animals propel themselves through water using a lateral undulation of their trunk, where the tail generates thrust by pushing against the fluid. Our findings indicate that the centipede's body mass is sufficiently low that drag forces dominate over inertial forces, allowing us to model its swimming dynamics using the quasi-steady approximation. Furthermore, we show that the centipede's body shape is optimized for efficient locomotion, as it achieves its maximum swimming speed at the frequency of undulation that minimizes the cost of transport. Finally, we compare the swimming mechanics of *T. geayi* with those of other water swimmers, revealing that this species exhibits unique characteristics, particularly in its tail morphology and swimming speed. These results provide valuable insights into the locomotion of aquatic animals and may inspire the design of bio-inspired swimming robots. This study examines the tsunami generated by the Chicxulub impactor, which caused the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event. The primary objective is to simulate the tsunami's propagation from the deep ocean to the shallow coastal regions of the Yucatan Peninsula. To achieve this, we employ the Non-hydrostatic Shallow Water Equations (NLSWE) within a two-way adaptive mesh refinement framework. This approach utilizes a hybrid grid system that combines a Cartesian mesh for the deep ocean with a curvilinear mesh for the shallow coastal area. The NLSWE model incorporates non-hydrostatic pressure terms to account for vertical accelerations and non-hydrostatic wave effects. We present results from a simulation that begins with a single grid resolution and progressively adapts to three different resolutions. These results demonstrate that the adaptive simulation successfully captures the tsunami's propagation and inundation across both deep and shallow domains. Furthermore, the simulation accurately reproduces the tsunami's reflection off the Yucatan Peninsula and its subsequent inundation of the region. Finally, we compare the adaptive simulation with a non-adaptive simulation to evaluate the impact of adaptive mesh refinement on the simulation's accuracy and computational efficiency. The findings indicate that the adaptive simulation achieves comparable accuracy to the non-adaptive version while requiring significantly less computational time. We present early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of IRAS F110-2301, a luminous infrared galaxy (LIRG) located at $z=0.031$ that exhibits no detectable optical emission. This object is notable for its extreme infrared luminosity ($L_{\rm IR} \sim 10^{12} L_{\odot}$) combined with a very low stellar mass ($M_{\star} \sim 10^{9} M_{\odot}$), suggesting it may represent a rare, early-stage LIRG. Our analysis of JWST NIRCam and NIRSpec data reveals that the infrared light is dominated by a single, compact stellar population ($\sim 100$ pc) with a stellar mass of $M_{\star} \sim 10^{9} M_{\odot}$ and a star formation rate of $\sim 10 M_{\odot} \rm{yr}^{-1}$. The spectral energy distribution (SED) indicates a young stellar population with a median age of $\sim 100$ Myr and a metallicity of $\sim 0.2 Z_{\odot}$. Furthermore, the presence of a strong [Ne V] $\lambda$3426 emission line in the NIRSpec data points to the existence of a hot accretion flow, likely driven by a supermassive black hole with a mass of $\sim 10^{7} M_{\odot}$. These findings suggest that IRAS F110-2301 is a prototypical LIRG, characterized by a massive starburst and an active galactic nucleus (AGN) that is currently obscured by dust. This study underscores the critical role of JWST in identifying and characterizing such early-stage LIRGs, which are essential for understanding the evolution of massive galaxies. Additionally, we highlight the necessity of conducting a systematic survey of optically dark, infrared-bright galaxies to better comprehend the formation and evolution of LIRGs.
