We examine the most general seven-dimensional gravity theory constructed solely from the Riemann tensor and its derivatives. Our analysis demonstrates that the most general four-derivative Lagrangian can be derived from a single action principle, whereas the most general five-derivative Lagrangian lacks such an action formulation. Furthermore, we establish that the most general seven-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity model—including all possible scalar couplings—admits a unique action only when the Gauss-Bonnet coupling constant takes a specific value. Additionally, we identify the most general scalar-coupled Gauss-Bonnet gravity theory that can be obtained from a single action. Finally, we provide the equations of motion for both the most general four-derivative and scalar-coupled six-derivative gravity theories. In the final section, we explore the implications of these findings for the low-energy effective actions of M-theory and its various string theory limits. Specifically, we show that the low-energy effective actions of M-theory, M(2,2), M(2,4), and M(2,6) can be derived from a single action up to the six-derivative level. However, for M(2,2) and M(2,4), this action formulation breaks down at the seven-derivative level, whereas for M(2,6), it persists up to the eight-derivative level. These results align with the conjecture that the low-energy effective action of M-theory is determined by the geometry of its moduli space. Moreover, we demonstrate that the low-energy effective action of M(2,6) can be derived from a single action up to the eight-derivative level, a finding that supports the conjecture that the moduli space of M(2,6) is homogeneous. Finally, we note that our findings regarding M(2,6) are consistent with the conjecture that the low-energy effective action of the type IIB superstring is determined by the geometry of its moduli space. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the low-energy effective action of the type IIB superstring can be derived from a single action up to the eight-derivative level. Additionally, we observe that the low-energy effective action of the type I superstring can be derived from a single action up to the six-derivative level, which is consistent with the conjecture that the low-energy effective action of the heterotic superstring is determined by the geometry of its moduli space.

This study examines the distinct impacts of different El Niño flavors on seasonal precipitation extremes across the globe. By analyzing the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre v2.0 dataset from 1901 to 2018, we identified the 10 wettest and 10 driest seasons for each region. We then classified the El Niño events occurring during these extreme seasons into three categories: unique flavors (appearing in only one extreme season), shared flavors (appearing in multiple extreme seasons), and non-occurring flavors (never appearing in any extreme season). Our results indicate that the spatial patterns of these unique flavors differ significantly between very wet and very dry seasons. Furthermore, the spatial patterns of shared flavors in extreme seasons are more similar to those of unique flavors than to the patterns of flavors that never occur during extremes. These findings suggest that the spatial distribution of precipitation extremes is influenced by the specific flavor of the El Niño event. This approach utilizes a recently developed theory of the scattering of non-linear waves, which offers a more comprehensive description of wave propagation in disordered media compared to the conventional weak scattering approximation. Furthermore, we illustrate that this theory can be applied to investigate the growth of non-affine growth modes in glasses. Uncertainty is inherent in most industrial environments, and the rise of Industry 4.0 has made it increasingly probable that data regarding uncertain parameters will be available. This study examines the scheduling of jobs on parallel machines, where job processing times are uncertain and modeled using either discrete or continuous probability distributions. We introduce a novel mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation that incorporates the probability of tardiness for each job, regardless of whether the underlying uncertainty is discrete or continuous. This approach enables the optimization of a robust objective function that accounts for the stochastic nature of processing times. To validate the model's effectiveness, we conducted computational experiments comparing its performance against a standard deterministic scheduling model. The results demonstrate that the proposed MILP model is highly effective and efficient, capable of solving instances with up to 100 jobs and 10 machines within a 3600-second time limit. Furthermore, the experiments reveal that modeling uncertainty in processing times yields substantial improvements in the average probability of tardiness. Finally, we observe that the advantages of the stochastic model over the deterministic one are more pronounced in scenarios with a higher number of machines. These findings suggest that stochastic programming is particularly beneficial in industrial contexts characterized by a large number of machines, such as assembly lines. Additionally, the stochastic model proves more advantageous when the degree of uncertainty is high, as indicated by a large coefficient of variation. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the stochastic model outperforms the deterministic one more significantly when the coefficient of variation is high. Consequently, the stochastic model is especially valuable in industrial settings where uncertainty is substantial, such as when machines are shared across multiple production lines. Finally, we note that the stochastic model is more advantageous when the number of scenarios is small, as the computational time required to solve the MILP increases with the number of scenarios. Therefore, the stochastic approach is most suitable when the number of scenarios is limited, such as when uncertainty arises from a small set of possible demand levels. In summary, the stochastic model is most beneficial when the number of scenarios is small, the number of machines is large, the coefficient of variation is high, and the number of jobs is large. These insights can guide decision-makers in selecting the most appropriate modeling approach for their specific industrial applications. The paper concludes with a discussion of these findings and potential avenues for future research. This study examines the statistical implications of the dynamical consistency of the Reynolds stress tensor in turbulent flows. We demonstrate that the probability density function (PDF) of the stress-to-strain rate ratio, denoted as $R$, exhibits a universal singularity at $R=1$. This finding holds true for both homogeneous and inhomogeneous turbulence, as well as for both statistically steady and non-stationary states. Furthermore, we show that the mean value of this ratio, $\langle R\rangle$, is strictly bounded below by 1, a result that contradicts the conventional assumption of a Gaussian distribution for the PDF of $R$. These conclusions are derived from a rigorous analysis of the dynamical consistency of the transport equation for the stress tensor, without relying on any modeling hypotheses. Additionally, we establish that the skewness of the PDF of $R$ is invariably negative, and we provide a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for turbulence modeling. Specifically, we propose a novel modeling approach that adheres to these theoretical constraints and validate it against direct numerical simulation data. Our results indicate that this new model significantly outperforms standard eddy-viscosity models in predicting the mean and variance of the stress-to-strain rate ratio. Moreover, the model demonstrates superior performance in predicting the mean and variance of the Reynolds shear stress across various canonical turbulent flows. These findings suggest that the proposed model holds significant potential for enhancing the accuracy of turbulence simulations in practical engineering applications. The source code for the model is available at https://github.com/abhisheksingh1996/Reynolds-stress-model. This approach is built upon the foundation of the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT), which is extended to incorporate effective operators that enable the creation of additional particles. Furthermore, we show that these operators can be constrained using existing experimental data. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity is a widely used method for investigating brain function and structure, as well as for diagnosing and treating various neurological conditions. However, the reliability of rs-fMRI connectivity findings remains uncertain, and the impact of data quality on these results is not well understood. This study addresses these gaps by examining the statistical strength and prediction accuracy of rs-fMRI connectivity across multiple sites. We analyzed data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) and the Abide dataset, which includes individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Our results indicate that prediction accuracy for rs-fMRI connectivity is highly dependent on the specific site, subject, and task. Furthermore, we observed that prediction accuracy for ASD subjects is generally lower than that for HCP subjects. These findings underscore the necessity of rigorous statistical validation when interpreting rs-fMRI connectivity. Additionally, we demonstrated that prediction accuracy can be enhanced by incorporating subject age and gender as covariates. Finally, we found that prediction accuracy improves when using a larger number of voxels, suggesting that voxel count is a critical factor influencing rs-fMRI connectivity prediction. These insights offer valuable guidance for future rs-fMRI research. The code used in this study is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/voxel_number. We introduce a naming algorithm designed for beeping networks, which operate under the constraints of asynchronous communication, limited memory, and the inability to transmit messages. This method ensures that every node successfully generates a unique identifier with a constant probability, while the total energy consumption remains proportional to the number of nodes. Our approach relies on a novel technique for estimating the network size, which we demonstrate is both necessary and sufficient for achieving energy-efficient naming in this context. Furthermore, we establish that any naming algorithm for beeping networks must incur energy costs at least proportional to the network size, thereby proving that our algorithm is optimal in terms of energy usage. Additionally, we present a randomized naming algorithm for beeping networks that achieves a running time proportional to the network size. This result improves upon the previously best-known algorithm, which had a running time of $O(n^2 \log n)$, and it is also optimal. Our findings are derived from a new analysis of the classic "coupon collector problem" within a distributed setting. Finally, we demonstrate that our algorithms can be adapted to the more general model of beeping networks that includes message capabilities, provided the message capacity is proportional to the network size. In this extended model, both the running time and energy consumption of our algorithms remain proportional to the number of nodes. To our knowledge, this represents the first algorithm for beeping networks that achieves optimality in both running time and energy consumption. Our results also imply that the previously best-known algorithm for beeping networks with message capacity is not optimal. We further show that our algorithm for beeping networks with message capacity can be extended to the model of beeping networks with communication, where nodes are permitted to send messages of arbitrary size. Positional encodings are essential for pre-trained language models to capture word order, yet they are often omitted in code-mixed language models due to the assumption that individual words within a mixed segment are too short to require such encoding. This paper introduces PESTO, a method for adaptive and relative positional encoding in code-mixed languages. PESTO dynamically adjusts the positional encoding scheme based on the "switching point" between languages within a sentence. We demonstrate that this approach yields state-of-the-art performance on the primary task of predicting mixed-language sentiment. Additionally, we show that PESTO effectively enhances other downstream tasks, including named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging. Our findings indicate that the proposed adaptive and relative positional encoding is particularly effective for code-mixed languages characterized by a higher frequency of code-mixing. This study employs first-principles calculations to analyze the pressure-dependent isotope effect and critical temperature ($T_c$) in H$_3$S hydride superconductors. By utilizing the Eliashberg theory of strong-coupling superconductivity, we compute the $T_c$ values for various pressures and isotopic masses. Our findings indicate that the isotope effect coefficient ($\alpha$) varies with pressure, reaching a maximum of 0.7 at 150 GPa. Furthermore, we observe that the pressure-induced van Hove singularity (vHS) significantly influences both the isotope effect and the $T_c$ of H$_3$S hydride superconductors. Specifically, the vHS causes a sharp decline in $\alpha$ and a corresponding increase in $T_c$. These results offer valuable insights into the superconducting properties of H$_3$S hydride superconductors. Additionally, our theoretical predictions align well with existing experimental data. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of these results for other high-temperature superconductors. Motion planning in dynamic environments is a critical challenge for mobile robots. This paper introduces a new method for generating spatial restrictions to facilitate motion planning amidst moving obstacles. The proposed approach comprises two main components: a spatial restriction generation module and a motion planning module. The former identifies spatial restrictions that prevent collisions with moving obstacles, while the latter plans robot motion based on these restrictions. To validate the method's effectiveness, simulations were conducted using a mobile robot navigating a 2D environment populated with moving obstacles. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach successfully generates spatial restrictions and plans collision-free trajectories. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness against variations in obstacle motion patterns and demonstrates high computational efficiency. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future research directions. We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve, together with a specified divisor, is finitely generated as a semifield over the tropical semifield $\mathbb{T} = (\mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty\}, \min, +)$. This result yields a finite basis for the divisorial valuations of the function field of a tropical curve and establishes the finite basis property for rank one divisorial valuation fields of tropical curves. Furthermore, we provide an effective upper bound for the number of elements required in a generating set. Our proof relies on the observation that the finiteness of the rank one divisor class group of a tropical curve is equivalent to the finite basis property for the rational function semifield of that curve. Additionally, we present a counterexample showing that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve is not necessarily finitely generated over $\mathbb{T}$ when the genus exceeds one. Finally, we offer a counterexample to the conjecture that the divisorial valuations of the function field of a tropical curve possess a finite basis in the general case. These findings are achieved through a novel approach to tropical divisors that circumvents the challenges posed by the lack of additivity in the degree function on a tropical curve. We anticipate that this new method will prove valuable for future research in tropical geometry. We conducted a theoretical investigation into the potential for nematic instability in LiFeAs, utilizing a model derived from first-principles calculations. By employing the random phase approximation, we determined the spin susceptibility and identified the wave vector that maximizes it. Our results indicate that the susceptibility reaches its peak at the zone center, with no instability occurring at the wave vector associated with the nematic phase. This finding aligns with experimental data, which show that the nematic phase transition in LiFeAs is driven by structural instabilities rather than electronic instabilities. Furthermore, we observed that the susceptibility is highly sensitive to the electron count per Fe atom, suggesting that LiFeAs could exhibit nematic instability under conditions of electron doping. Finally, we compared the spin susceptibility of LiFeAs with that of BaFe2As2, revealing that the maximum susceptibility in the latter occurs at the wave vector linked to the nematic phase. This distinction supports the hypothesis that nematicity in BaFe2As2 arises from electronic instabilities. Additionally, we examined the impact of spin-orbit coupling on the susceptibility, finding that it significantly alters the susceptibility near the zone center. These results underscore the critical role of spin-orbit coupling in the nematic phase transition of LiFeAs. Overall, our study demonstrates that the nematic phase transition in LiFeAs is primarily structural, whereas it is electronic in nature for BaFe2As2. These findings offer valuable insights into the nematic phase transition in iron-based superconductors. The source code for the calculations is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1999/LiFeAs. This study examines the global alignment limit within two-Higgs-doublet models, utilizing projected results from future collider experiments. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of the most promising future facilities, including the High-Luminosity LHC, HE-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, and CEPC, to determine their sensitivity to the Yukawa couplings of the light CP-even Higgs boson. Our findings indicate that the HL-LHC will achieve a 10% precision level, whereas the HE-LHC, FCC-ee, ILC, CLIC, and CEPC are expected to reach approximately 1% accuracy. Furthermore, the FCC-hh, operating at both 100 TeV and 75 TeV, will deliver an accuracy of roughly 0.1%. These outcomes demonstrate that the alignment limit can be experimentally verified across all these future collider scenarios. Additionally, we explore the potential for discovering additional Higgs bosons at these facilities, with a particular focus on the CP-odd Higgs boson. Our analysis reveals that the HL-LHC will probe a mass range of 100–1000 GeV with a sensitivity of 0.1, while the HE-LHC, FCC-ee, ILC, CLIC, and CEPC will achieve sensitivities of approximately 0.01. Finally, the FCC-hh will offer an accuracy of about 0.001 for masses between 10 and 1000 GeV. These results suggest that the discovery of additional Higgs bosons is feasible at all these future collider options. In conclusion, our findings underscore the critical importance of these future colliders for advancing our understanding of the Higgs sector. This approach enables the creation of materials with diverse structures and symmetries, including linear chains, rings, and various polyhedral forms such as tetrahedrons, cubes, and octahedrons. Furthermore, the neural network interactions can be adapted to form networks and sheets. The methodology is demonstrated using a single neural network and a multi-layer network, with the latter proving more effective at preventing particle aggregation. Additionally, we show that the neural network-based strategies can be combined with a reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize the self-assembly process. This neuroevolutionary strategy successfully generates the most compact structures, achieving the highest density. Our findings indicate that the reinforcement learning algorithm is highly effective in accelerating the self-assembly process. Overall, our results demonstrate that the proposed neuroevolutionary strategy is versatile and capable of producing a wide range of materials. We investigate robustness within chiral gauge theories, demonstrating that robustness emerges when the theory is formulated in a specific gauge. Furthermore, we establish that the phase structure of chiral gauge theories is governed by the same anomaly inflow mechanism found in chiral topological insulators. This finding enables the systematic classification of chiral gauge theories, revealing that certain models undergo phase transitions to trivial phases at specific coupling strengths. Additionally, we identify that some theories possess a phase boundary with topological gauge theories, while others exhibit phase transitions to non-trivial topological gauge theories. Finally, we explore the relationship between the phase structure of chiral gauge theories and the bulk-boundary correspondence. In this context, we demonstrate that the phase structure of chiral gauge theories is intrinsically linked to the boundary phase of the topological insulator. This connection offers a novel method for determining the phase structure of chiral gauge theories. As an application, we utilize this approach to analyze the phase structure of a specific chiral gauge theory. Our findings indicate that this theory features a phase boundary with a topological gauge theory and a phase boundary with a topological insulator. These results are supported by numerical simulations. Our work provides a comprehensive framework for classifying chiral gauge theories and elucidates the boundary phase of topological insulators. This framework is anticipated to facilitate the discovery of new chiral gauge theories and to deepen our understanding of their phase structures. Finally, we discuss the potential for constructing new topological phases of matter using chiral gauge theories. Specifically, we propose that chiral gauge theories can serve as effective descriptions for topological phases of matter. This insight may guide the search for novel topological phases of matter. Overall, our findings offer a systematic approach for classifying chiral gauge theories and elucidate their phase structures. This paper examines the stationary Navier-Stokes equations within unbounded domains of $\mathbb{R}^3$. We establish that these equations are generally ill-posed when considering initial data in essential Besov spaces $B_{\infty,1}^{1}$ and $B_{\infty,1}^{0}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ill-posedness also occurs for data in the space $B_{\infty,1}^{1}$ under the slip boundary condition. These findings are derived through a direct construction of a sequence of initial data that converges to zero in the norm of the respective space, yet generates a sequence of solutions that fails to converge to zero in any distributional sense. Additionally, we prove that the ill-posedness of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in $B_{\infty,1}^{1}$ is equivalent to the ill-posedness of the heat equation with the same initial data space. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the well-posedness of the time-dependent Navier-Stokes equations. The methodology employed relies on the characterization of the Helmholtz projection in essential Besov spaces, as detailed in our prior work. This approach may also be applicable to other ill-posedness problems involving the Helmholtz projection. Notably, this study marks the first instance of ill-posedness for the stationary Navier-Stokes equations being established through a direct construction. Previous investigations into this problem had utilized indirect methods, such as the blow-up criterion for time-dependent Navier-Stokes equations or the relationship between the stationary and time-dependent formulations. Our direct construction technique offers a more straightforward and effective approach to demonstrating ill-posedness. Moreover, this method can be extended to address other problems where the ill-posedness of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations is a critical component. The paper concludes with a discussion of these broader implications. Overall, this work underscores the significance of the ill-posedness of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in essential Besov spaces and highlights the potential for future research in this area. This matrix is defined as a generalized Gabidulin matrix, characterized by the property that for any vector $u \in \mathcal{C}$, the rank of $Mu$ equals the rank of $u$. Furthermore, the performance of the cryptosystem is compared against the original version of Loidreau's scheme. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. We demonstrate that the behavior of minimal spanning acycles in random complexes mirrors that of minimal spanning trees in random graphs, as established by Bollobas, Janson, and Riordan. Furthermore, we derive mass laws for both minimal spanning acycles and persistence diagrams within random complexes, alongside extremal laws for minimal spanning acycles in random graphs. Additionally, we examine the random simplex complex, where we establish a phase transition regarding the emergence of a giant component in the persistence diagram. Finally, we present a minimal spanning forest model for graphs, which extends the minimal spanning tree framework to weighted graphs. In this context, we prove that the extremal laws for minimal spanning forests align with those of minimal spanning acycles in random complexes. This finding confirms the conjecture proposed by Bollobas, Janson, and Riordan concerning the extremal law of minimal spanning forests on complete graphs. The methodology employed relies on the Janson-Szemerédi theorem and the concept of $k$-core. The paper concludes with an analysis of the random simplex complex, where we demonstrate that the extremal law of the minimal spanning forest corresponds to that of the minimal spanning tree. This result is derived from a novel random graph model featuring a giant component, which is subsequently utilized to prove the aforementioned findings. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-preserving collaborative machine learning framework where participants share only vertical data slices with a leader to jointly train models. While VFL offers significant privacy advantages, it remains vulnerable to various attacks. This paper introduces a suite of practical privacy assaults targeting VFL, encompassing model inversion, membership inference, and data reconstruction attacks. We demonstrate that these threats are feasible against both tree-based and linear VFL models. Furthermore, we evaluate the efficacy of existing defense mechanisms, revealing that they are largely ineffective against these specific attacks. Our findings indicate that even when participants employ differential privacy, the VFL framework still fails to provide adequate privacy guarantees. Finally, we explore the potential of federated graph neural networks as a more robust alternative for ensuring privacy in collaborative learning environments. We investigate the exclusive decay of $B$ mesons into a proton and a dark antibaryon, where the dark sector is modeled as a hidden $SU(3)_F$ flavor symmetry. By employing QCD light-cone sum rules, we derive expressions for the $B$-meson decay form factors in terms of QCD light-cone distribution amplitudes. These amplitudes are defined by the nonperturbative probability amplitudes for finding the proton's quark constituents at a specific light-cone time. Utilizing these results, we establish constraints on the dark antibaryon mass based on the observed non-existence of $B$ meson decays into dark antibaryons. Furthermore, we analyze the potential for detecting dark antibaryons through $B$ meson decays at the Belle II experiment. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for dark matter direct detection experiments. This work is part of the Belle II Physics Beyond the Standard Model Working Group. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective for node classification, yet they often struggle with limited labeled data. The AWAKE experiment at CERN's LHC aims to demonstrate beam-induced coherent emission of wakefield radiation by injecting a beam of proton bunches into a beam of high-intensity, high-energy protons. This study examines the potential for detecting X-ray emission resulting from the betatron oscillations of a low-energy proton beam as it traverses a plasma channel generated by the high-energy proton beam. The investigation explores the feasibility of observing this betatron radiation using the LHC's ALICE X-ray detector. Furthermore, the study analyzes the radiation's sensitivity to plasma density fluctuations and its dependence on the energy and transverse size of the injected proton beam. These factors are critical for optimizing the beam parameters required to detect betatron radiation within the ALICE X-ray detector. The research concludes that the betatron radiation emitted by protons with a 100 MeV energy and a 100 $\mu$m transverse size, propagating through a plasma channel with a density of $10^{17}$ cm$^{-3}$, is detectable by the ALICE X-ray detector. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the radiation's spectral peak can be tuned to the detector's most sensitive energy range by adjusting the plasma density. Finally, the study confirms that the betatron radiation is highly sensitive to plasma density fluctuations, which can be leveraged to measure these fluctuations with high precision. This sensitivity is particularly valuable for optimizing the plasma channel to maximize the detection of betatron radiation. The findings of this study will inform the design of future experiments to detect and characterize betatron radiation in the AWAKE Run 2 phase. This study examines the optimization of regularized Rényi divergence, a non-convex objective function that generalizes Kullback-Leibler divergence and finds applications in information retrieval, machine learning, and statistics. We introduce Bregman proximal gradient algorithms to address this optimization, demonstrating that these methods converge to the unique stationary point of the problem. Furthermore, we establish that the algorithms achieve global convergence when the objective function is strongly convex. Finally, we present numerical experiments comparing our approach to existing methods in the literature. These results indicate that our proposed algorithms are competitive and, in certain scenarios, superior to current state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we show that our method outperforms the Kullback-Leibler divergence in specific cases. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. This work examines a dynamical system featuring inertia and damping, where the Tikhonov regularization parameter diminishes over time. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, this system converges asymptotically to the minimum-norm solution of an inclusion problem. Furthermore, we establish the convergence rate toward this solution and illustrate the findings with numerical examples. These results extend previous literature, which typically focused on convergence to the set of minimizers without guaranteeing a limit point, or which ensured convergence to a single minimizer but failed to identify it as the least norm solution. Additionally, our approach accommodates a broader range of operator classes, including those that are merely maximally monotone or firmly nonexpansive. Finally, we explore the link between our findings and the well-established Nesterov method for convex optimization. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews essential background concepts; Section 3 addresses inclusion problems with maximally monotone operators; Section 4 covers firmly nonexpansive operators; Section 5 applies these results to convex optimization; and Section 6 presents numerical examples. Wall-following robots, which rely on tactile sensors to navigate corridors, are prone to disorderly transitions into chaotic motion when environmental parameters such as corridor width or robot size vary. This study examines the nature of this chaos and the mechanisms driving the transition. We demonstrate that the system exhibits two distinct types of chaos: one characterized by a single attractor and another by multiple attractors. Furthermore, we show that the system's dynamics can be reduced to a one-dimensional map, enabling the identification of a period-doubling route to chaos. Finally, we establish that the observed transition to chaos is of the border-collision type. These findings are validated through numerical simulations and experiments conducted on a physical robot. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for the design of wall-following robots. We investigate the impact of extended impurities on the energy-dependent microwave conductivity of kinetic energy-driven conductors, specifically focusing on the crossover from diffusive to ballistic transport. Plants are essential to human survival, yet they require specific environmental conditions to thrive. While environmental factors like light, temperature, and humidity are critical, the spatial arrangement of plants is equally vital; overcrowding can lead to competition for resources and stunted growth. Although humans possess the expertise to optimize plant spacing, automating this process for large-scale agricultural operations remains a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce GrowSpace, a system designed to learn how to cultivate plants by optimizing their spatial distribution. Our approach involves training a neural network to predict the optimal spacing for a given number of plants, thereby maximizing yield. We evaluated GrowSpace using a physics-based plant growth simulator, demonstrating that it can effectively learn appropriate spacing strategies. Furthermore, we show that GrowSpace can be deployed in real-world settings to automatically adjust planting intervals, offering a promising solution for efficient large-scale farming. We present a conformal welding approach to Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) on quantum disks, which yields a novel construction of the SLE loop. This method offers an alternative to the standard chordal SLE loop construction and provides a unified framework for defining SLE loops on quantum surfaces. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the definition of SLE loops on quantum cones, thereby extending the scope of the quantum cone loop measure. Finally, we demonstrate that the resulting SLE loop measure satisfies the necessary gluing equations. This research is conducted in collaboration with Alexander Berestycki. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive exposition of the quantum cone loop measure, including its scaling limits, and explore its connections to the uniform infinite planar triangulation (UIPT) and the uniform infinite half-plane triangulation (UIHPT). These findings are based on a joint project with Alexander Berestycki. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the quantum cone loop measure; Section 3 examines its scaling limits; and Section 4 investigates its relationship with the UIPT and UIHPT. We demonstrate that the curvaton mechanism can generate primordial black holes (PBHs) with masses ranging from $10^{-16}$ to $10^{6}M_{\odot}$. In this framework, the inflaton and curvaton fields operate sequentially, with the curvaton subsequently decaying into dark matter. We show that PBHs can form during the early phase of curvaton evolution, driven by a non-Gaussian component within the curvature perturbation. Furthermore, we establish a correlation between the abundance of PBHs and dark matter, indicating that the curvaton field can simultaneously account for both. Finally, we examine the constraints imposed by Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) and Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) anisotropies, finding that the model remains viable across a broad parameter space. Additionally, we note that the curvaton's decay can produce a significant isocurvature perturbation, which may be detectable by future CMB experiments. This approach offers a novel method for generating PBHs and represents the first instance of such production via an oscillating curvaton. Consequently, it provides a promising avenue for investigating the early universe and the formation of primordial black holes. This study introduces a new method for analyzing longitudinal educational data, utilizing the National Education Longitudinal Study of 2000 (NELS:2000) as a case study. The approach employs a latent variable model to estimate the probability of students following specific academic trajectories, such as enrolling in college, completing a degree, or entering the workforce. By integrating these model estimates with observed covariates, the research calculates the impact of various factors on trajectory selection. The findings indicate that while race and parental education levels significantly influence choices, the effects of gender and family income are negligible. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that including additional covariates can substantially alter the estimated influence of race and parental education. Finally, the paper discusses the advantages of this methodology for examining academic pathways and suggests potential future applications. The authors acknowledge that this work was partially supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. 0835892. The data used in this study can be accessed at http://nces.ed.gov/nelsed/. The analysis was conducted using R (R Core Team, 2017). Additional details regarding the methodology are provided in Martinez and Kline (2018). The R package 'mice' (van Buuren et al., 2018) was utilized for multiple imputation, and the 'lavaan' package (Rosseel, 2012) facilitated the estimation of the latent variable models. The 'survey' package (Lumley, 2014) was employed to account for the complex sampling design. Finally, the 'ggplot2' package (Wickham, 2009) was used to generate the figures.

This study introduces a vehicle platoon formation control framework utilizing differential games. The proposed method enables each vehicle to independently and automatically generate a formation by solving a local differential game. Furthermore, the approach offers linked control, ensuring that the relative positions of vehicles remain consistent even when communication is disrupted. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Additionally, the paper discusses the relationship between this method and existing approaches, such as the leader-follower formation control strategy. Finally, the study addresses the issue of multiple equilibria and proposes a technique to select the most suitable equilibrium point. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Linked-and-Automated-Vehicle-Platoon-Formation-Control. This study examines interaction effects within logistic regression models. We demonstrate that interaction terms are unnecessary when analyzing the relationship between a single predictor and a binary outcome. Furthermore, for multiple predictors, interactions are required only to capture the joint influence of all variables on the outcome. In cases where predictors are correlated, interactions may be needed to prevent omitted variable bias. Finally, we illustrate how interactions can be utilized to identify subgroups of individuals who respond differently to a treatment. The paper concludes with a discussion of the findings. An accompanying R package, `nointer`, is available to facilitate the implementation of these concepts. The code for this work can be found at https://github.com/andreasgustafsson/nointer. The authors' data are accessible at https://github.com/andreasgustafsson/nointer/tree/master/data. Keywords: Logistic regression, interactions, treatment effects, subgroup analysis. The proliferation of automatically generated headlines on the web has become a significant issue, as these summaries often lack quality and fail to capture the full essence of the original content. This study introduces a method for detecting such headlines by leveraging pre-trained transformer models. Our approach utilizes the sentence-level representations generated by these models to classify headlines. Experimental results demonstrate that transformer-based methods outperform other state-of-the-art techniques, achieving an F1 score of 0.89. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/transformer-headline-detection. Additionally, we have released a dataset comprising 100,000 news articles, which can be downloaded from https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/transformer-headline-detection. This dataset will serve as the foundation for the Automated Headline Detection (AHD) challenge at the 11th Workshop on Computational Linguistics for the Social Media (WCLS-2021). The workshop will take place in conjunction with the 55th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL) in Yokohama, Japan, from July 11 to 16, 2021. The AHD challenge is scheduled to occur on July 14, 2021. For further details, please visit https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/transformer-headline-detection. We present a comprehensive study of chiral spin liquids (CSLs) across amorphous and polycrystalline spin systems, utilizing both classical and quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our findings indicate that CSLs can be realized in amorphous systems, whereas they are absent in polycrystalline systems composed of ferromagnetic CSL grains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the boundaries between these two regimes are defined by a first-order phase transition. Finally, we explore the potential for detecting CSLs in real materials through neutron scattering experiments. This research is motivated by the recent proposal of a CSL phase in the kagome metal $YbCu_2O_5$. Our results suggest that the CSL phase in this material is likely to be polycrystalline, thereby challenging the original proposal. Additionally, we propose that neutron scattering experiments could be conducted to verify the existence of CSL in $YbCu_2O_5$. Finally, we examine the broader implications of our findings for the search for CSL phases in other materials. Our analysis indicates that the presence of grain boundaries in polycrystalline systems poses a significant obstacle to the realization of CSL phases. Consequently, our study underscores the necessity of single crystals for investigating CSL phases. This conclusion is supported by the recent successful synthesis of single crystals of $YbCu_2O_5$. We anticipate that our findings will guide future experimental efforts to identify CSL phases in materials. Ultimately, our work provides a theoretical framework for comprehending the physics of CSL phases in both amorphous and polycrystalline systems. This study contributes to the ongoing quest for new quantum materials and technologies, with CSL phases representing a promising avenue for the development of novel quantum devices. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to generate portfolio distributions for out-of-sample data. The system utilizes an autoencoding conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to create synthetic portfolio distributions based on input data. To evaluate the quality of these synthetic distributions, we employ the Wasserstein distance and the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). Furthermore, we assess the framework's performance by applying the Conditional Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (CnDCG) metric. Experimental results indicate that our approach effectively generates portfolio distributions that closely resemble the original out-of-sample data. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed method can enhance the performance of existing portfolio optimization techniques. This study presents the application of Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) to classify blazar sources from the Fermi-LAT catalog. The dataset comprises 1,000 sources, evenly split between 500 BL Lacertae objects and 500 Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars (FSQs), selected from the 3LAC catalog. The model was trained using the gamma-ray spectral energy distribution (SED) of each source, represented by a histogram of photon counts across 100 energy bins spanning 0.1 GeV to 10 TeV. The results indicate that the Bayesian neural network achieves a classification accuracy of 98.6%, surpassing the 97.5% accuracy of a standard feed-forward neural network. Furthermore, the Bayesian approach provides a measure of classification uncertainty, which is particularly valuable for sources located near the decision boundary. This research demonstrates that Bayesian neural networks are a robust method for classifying blazar sources. Additionally, the study confirms that the Bayesian framework is more effective than the standard feed-forward approach at identifying sources with uncertain classifications. Social media has become a vital tool for individuals with disabilities to connect with their communities. However, the diversity of platforms and the complexity of their interfaces often create barriers, hindering users from creating and sharing digital content. This study examines the experiences of people with disabilities regarding social media content creation. Through a qualitative analysis of 100 interviews conducted in English, Spanish, and French, we identify key obstacles and opportunities. Our findings reveal that while social media offers significant benefits, users face challenges related to usability, accessibility, and a lack of awareness regarding available tools. We propose a framework to guide future research and development aimed at enhancing social media for these communities. Furthermore, we outline specific recommendations for platform designers and developers to improve content authoring processes. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for usability and accessibility professionals. This research is part of a broader initiative involving over 1,000 participants across 20 countries, with this paper focusing on a subset of those responses. The complete dataset will be made available to the research community. Additionally, we have established a community of practice to foster ongoing dialogue and collaboration among people with disabilities regarding social media. This community is open to anyone interested in supporting individuals with disabilities in utilizing social media. This paper introduces the tensor merge of hypergraphs, which extends the tensor product of graphs, and investigates its spectral characteristics. We demonstrate that the singular values of a hypergraph's adjacency tensor are derived from the eigenvalues of its adjacency tensor, and we establish that the spectrum of the adjacency tensor for a hypergraph consists of fourth powers. Furthermore, we examine the spectral radius and signless spectral radius of hypergraphs, noting that these values for specific hypergraphs can be arbitrarily large. Finally, we analyze the spectral properties of hypergraphs that are regular in both degree and edge size. Additionally, we present several examples of hypergraphs and discuss the challenges associated with classifying them. Finally, we outline several open problems for future research. This work serves as a foundation for further investigation into hypergraph theory.

We introduce a global optimization technique for locating dominant transition routes in complex systems, grounded in the principle of minimizing the Freidlin-Wentzell action. This approach is demonstrated through its application to the escape dynamics of a bistable system subject to multiplicative noise. We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV (M32-XXV), a new dwarf galaxy within the Andromeda group, identified through a deep survey of the Andromeda halo conducted with the VLT Survey Telescope. This object is located at a distance of 1.1 Mpc from the Andromeda galaxy and exhibits a high stellar density, with a half-light radius of 1.2 arcseconds. We present a new distance measurement of 1.10 ± 0.01 Mpc, derived from the analysis of 12 RR Lyrae variable stars. Additionally, we report the detection of 12 red giant branch stars, which allow for a distance modulus determination of 24.90 ± 0.02 mag. The galaxy displays a metallicity of [Fe/H] = -1.2 ± 0.2 dex and a low alpha-element abundance of [α/Fe] = -0.4 ± 0.2 dex. We identify a single globular cluster within the system, which has a metallicity of [Fe/H] = -1.6 ± 0.2 dex. Furthermore, we present a new radial velocity measurement of v_r = 200 ± 1 km/s. Based on these findings, we estimate the galaxy's mass within its half-light radius to be M(1/2r_h) = 1.1 +1.0 -0.5 × 10^7 M_sun, indicating a low central dark matter concentration. We also provide a new estimate for the Andromeda group's virial mass, M_200 = 1.1 +1.0 -0.5 × 10^12 M_sun. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the Andromeda group's formation and evolution. This is the 25th dwarf galaxy identified in the Andromeda group. Grant-free massive connectivity (GC) is a promising technique for Internet of Things (IoT) applications, enabling numerous devices to transmit data without requiring individual resource allocation. This paper introduces a two-stage genetic algorithm designed to generate non-orthogonal sequences for IoT devices. In the initial stage, the algorithm optimizes sequence length and sparsity to minimize the Hamming distance between sequences. Subsequently, in the second stage, it optimizes the number of symbols within each sequence to further reduce Hamming distance. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of Hamming distance, thereby enhancing the overall performance of grant-free massive connectivity systems. Additionally, the method exhibits superior robustness against channel estimation errors. Finally, the computational complexity of the proposed algorithm is significantly lower than that of other state-of-the-art methods. Consequently, this approach is highly suitable for IoT scenarios characterized by massive connectivity and limited device computational capabilities. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmadreza123456/Non-orthogonal-sequences.

This study examines various approximations of the thermodynamic properties of moist air, specifically focusing on the moist air equation of state and enthalpy. It demonstrates that the standard approximation for the moist air equation of state fails to satisfy the thermodynamic stability condition, whereas an alternative formulation does. Furthermore, the analysis proves that the widely used approximation for moist air enthalpy is not thermodynamically coherent with this valid equation of state. Finally, the paper concludes by presenting a thermodynamically coherent set of approximations for both the moist air equation of state and enthalpy. These findings are particularly significant for applications involving the numerical solution of the Euler equations for moist air. In such contexts, the equation of state is typically solved iteratively to determine dry-bulb temperature, while enthalpy is often calculated using the standard approximation. Consequently, the temperature derived from the iterative process may not correspond to the true thermodynamic temperature implied by the approximate enthalpy value. This discrepancy can result in violations of the second law of thermodynamics when solving the Euler equations. The proposed solution is to employ a thermodynamically coherent set of approximations for both the equation of state and enthalpy. This approach ensures that the temperature obtained from the iterative solution of the equation of state is consistent with the enthalpy approximation, thereby guaranteeing adherence to the second law. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the practical implications of these results. The paper also references existing literature on the thermodynamic properties of moist air and includes an appendix detailing the derivation of the proposed thermodynamically coherent approximations. Additionally, the appendix presents a method for determining the coefficients of these approximations based on the thermodynamic properties of dry air and water vapor. This methodology is applied to the coefficients of the approximations used in the Weather Research and Forecasting model. This paper introduces a method for modeling ASR ambiguity during dialogue state tracking by integrating ASR confidence scores with a novel probabilistic framework for interpreting Word Confusion Networks (WCNs). We demonstrate that incorporating WCNs into the dialogue state tracking model enhances performance across all three evaluated datasets. Furthermore, we find that WCNs are particularly beneficial for handling ASR ambiguities related to word order and repetition. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed WCN-based approach yields performance gains comparable to those achieved by the more complex and computationally intensive Reranking method. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1997/WCN-DCG.

Keywords: Dialogue State Tracking, Word Confusion Networks, ASR Ambiguity, Probabilistic Modeling.

We establish a general formula for the number of algebraically stable, effective, and globally generated bundles on a smooth projective curve, ordered by their rank and degree. This approach relies on a combinatorial description of the space of such bundles, originally proposed by Balaji and Seshadri. As applications, we determine the count of these bundles for specific low-rank cases, including vector bundles on smooth projective curves with rank 2 and degree up to 10, and rank 3 with degree up to 6. Additionally, we examine the scenario where the curve possesses non-trivial moduli. In this context, we demonstrate that the number of bundles of rank 2 and degree 6 is infinite whenever the curve's genus is at least 4. Finally, we present a formula for the number of globally generated, effective, algebraically stable bundles on a projective space, which applies to both ample and non-ample line bundles. This result yields a novel proof of a theorem by Aluffi and Carlsson regarding the Chern class of the tautological class on the Grassmannian. Furthermore, it confirms a conjecture by Aluffi and Carlsson concerning the non-negativity of these counts. The paper also includes an appendix by Ravi Vakil, which provides an alternative proof of the main result using a different combinatorial framework. This appendix also offers a combinatorial interpretation of the formula in terms of the Grothendieck class of the moduli space of these bundles. Our methodology is applicable to any projective space, though the resulting formulas become increasingly intricate as the dimension increases. We also explore the relationship between our findings and the work of Aluffi, Carlsson, and Petersen. Finally, we discuss several open questions and potential future research directions. We introduce a comprehensive framework for assessing entanglement within optical qubit systems. This approach utilizes a generalized Bell inequality, which is derived from the density matrix of the two-qubit system and subsequently tested through photon counting experiments. The method is validated using both pure and mixed entangled states, demonstrating that the optimal Bell inequality parameters can be determined analytically. Furthermore, we establish that these optimal parameters remain invariant under local unitary transformations. This protocol offers a straightforward and efficient means to evaluate entanglement in optical qubit systems, with potential applications in quantum communication and computing. Additionally, the technique can be extended to assess multipartite entanglement in systems involving more than two qubits. Finally, we outline a practical implementation of this method using a quantum dot source to generate entangled photon pairs. The proposed scheme is compatible with existing experimental setups and holds significant potential for real-world applications. This study examines the characteristics of a specific mode type, known as the "Palm Tree Mode" (PTM), observed in the JET tokamak. The analysis covers both the conditions under which these modes arise and their fundamental properties. The investigation utilizes a reduced model that incorporates the essential physics of PTMs, including their interaction with the background plasma state. This model is validated against experimental data from JET discharges. The research demonstrates that PTMs are driven by the coupling between the plasma and the wall, specifically through the interaction between the wall and the plasma's edge current. Furthermore, the study confirms that PTMs are non-resonant and non-ideal, meaning they are not governed by the ideal MHD dispersion relation. Finally, the paper outlines the potential for developing a predictive model for PTMs. These findings are crucial for understanding the impact of edge-localized modes on the performance of future tokamaks. Additionally, the proposed model could be applied to investigate similar modes in other tokamak devices. The source code for this model is accessible at https://github.com/andrewdavidson/PTM_model. Addressing Continual Learning (CL) is essential for deploying machine learning in real-world scenarios. While numerous methods have been proposed to mitigate CL challenges, the field currently lacks a standardized benchmark for fair comparison. This paper introduces a straightforward baseline that rivals state-of-the-art CL techniques relying on pretrained models. Our approach combines a simple rehearsal strategy with a novel, lightweight uncertainty-based mechanism to manage catastrophic forgetting. We evaluated our method against 11 state-of-the-art CL algorithms using both synthetic and real datasets, demonstrating that our baseline consistently outperforms these methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepLearningResearch/Continual-Learning-Benchmark. This work aims to establish a robust benchmark for future research in Continual Learning. This study examines how degree distribution heterogeneity influences the synchronization of integrate-and-fire neurons connected via random synapses. We demonstrate that networks with power-law degree distributions are more susceptible to synchronization than those with homogeneous degrees. Furthermore, we find that the critical coupling strength required for synchronization is independent of the network size. Finally, we show that the transition to synchronization is continuous and that the critical coupling strength scales with the second moment of the degree distribution. These findings are validated through numerical simulations. Additionally, we derive an analytical expression for the critical coupling strength, which aligns well with simulation results for both homogeneous and power-law networks. This expression indicates that the critical coupling strength is directly proportional to the second moment of the degree distribution and inversely proportional to the sum of excitatory and inhibitory connection probabilities. We also provide an analytical estimate for the synchronization order parameter, which matches numerical results for power-law networks. Finally, we present an analytical expression for the synchronization threshold in networks of type-I neurons with power-law degree distributions. This expression reveals that the threshold is proportional to the second moment of the degree distribution and the connection probability, and inversely proportional to the network size. These results are confirmed by numerical simulations. Overall, our findings suggest that the second moment of the degree distribution is a key factor in determining the synchronization threshold. This insight could be valuable for designing neural networks with specific synchronization properties. Automatic Program Repair (APR) aims to identify and fix bugs in source code. While many APR techniques rely on analyzing program execution traces to derive repair rules, these traces are susceptible to adversarial inputs designed to mislead the repair process. This paper introduces a novel adversarial mask generation method that disrupts the correlation between program statements and faults by selectively masking execution traces. We evaluated this approach using the widely adopted GenFix dataset, which comprises Java programs with known repairs. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms the original GenFix dataset, achieving a 1.5% improvement in repair success rates. Furthermore, we conducted a case study to analyze the characteristics of the generated adversarial masks. The source code for our method is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/MaskGen. This work represents the first application of adversarial mask generation to the field of automatic program repair. The experimental results confirm that the method effectively hinders APR tools from locating bugs and successfully generates adversarial examples that expose the limitations of current APR techniques. Consequently, this research underscores the necessity of developing more robust APR tools capable of handling such adversarial scenarios. The paper concludes by outlining several promising directions for future work. The source code for our method is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/MaskGen. This study establishes a characterization for the capacity region of a general interference channel with common messages (GIFC), utilizing an information spectrum approach. This methodology enables the derivation of capacity region characterizations for sequence of channel models where traditional information-theoretic methods fail. The proposed achievable rate region is based on time-sharing among various input distributions, and it is demonstrated that this region indeed represents the capacity region of the GIFC. Furthermore, the findings of this work can be extended to generalized models of the two-user broadcast channel featuring common messages. Finally, the paper applies these results to specific interference channel models, yielding corresponding capacity region characterizations. Notably, this represents the first achievement in characterizing the capacity region for any interference channel model. Additionally, the application to the deterministic channel yields a characterization of its capacity region, thereby resolving an open problem. The methodology employed in this paper can be generalized to characterize the capacity regions of other channel models. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. The primary contributions of this work are as follows: 1) The development of an information spectrum method to characterize the capacity region of the GIFC; 2) The characterization of the capacity region for specific interference channel models; 3) The characterization of the capacity region for a two-user broadcast channel with common messages; and 4) The characterization of the capacity region for a deterministic channel. The significance of this work lies in its provision of the first capacity region characterization for any interference channel model. Moreover, the results offer a foundation for future research aimed at characterizing the capacity region of the general interference channel. The initial moments of relativistic heavy-ion collisions generate a quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a state of matter where quarks and gluons are no longer confined within hadrons. The QGP's characteristics are defined by its equation of state (EOS), which links pressure to energy density. This EOS is investigated using the newly developed 3-dimensional flow (3DF) observable. 3DF is derived from the flow coefficients $v_n$ and $r_n$, which are extracted from the azimuthal anisotropy of the final-state particle distribution. The relationship between 3DF and the QGP's EOS is established through viscous hydrodynamic simulations. These simulations employ a novel viscosity model that incorporates the temperature dependence of shear viscosity, $\eta/s$, and the bulk viscosity, $\kappa/s$, alongside a parameterized EOS. The findings indicate that 3DF is highly sensitive to the EOS and the temperature dependence of $\eta/s$ and $\kappa/s$. Furthermore, 3DF is found to be less affected by fluctuations in the initial energy density profile compared to other flow observables. Consequently, 3DF serves as a valuable tool for constraining the QGP's EOS and viscosity properties. This study also examines the 3DF's response to variations in the initial conditions and the impact of event-by-event fluctuations. Finally, 3DF is compared with experimental data from the ALICE collaboration for central Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 2.76$ TeV and 5.02 TeV, as well as for central Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 2.76$ TeV. The results demonstrate that 3DF is in good agreement with the ALICE data. These findings suggest that the temperature dependence of $\eta/s$ and $\kappa/s$ can be constrained using 3DF, and that the QGP's EOS can be determined with a precision of approximately 10%. This level of accuracy is comparable to that achieved by other flow observables. The 3DF observable is expected to be measured in future heavy-ion collision experiments, such as those at the LHC and RHIC. Additionally, 3DF is anticipated to be a valuable tool for studying the QGP in future heavy-ion collision facilities, including the FAIR, NICA, and J-PARC. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant global disruption, with early detection of infected individuals being a critical component of containment strategies. However, the widespread adoption of deep learning for this purpose is hindered by privacy concerns, as such models often require access to sensitive patient data. This study introduces a novel framework for training deep neural networks to identify COVID-19 cases while safeguarding patient privacy. Our approach employs adversarial training to generate synthetic data that preserves the statistical characteristics of the original dataset. We evaluate the efficacy of these synthetic datasets in training robust deep neural networks for early detection. Experimental results demonstrate that our method enables the development of high-performance deep neural networks for early COVID-19 detection using synthetic data, without compromising patient privacy. Furthermore, we show that the proposed framework can be applied to other domains, such as medical image classification. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for solving complex problems in wireless transmission systems, offering the potential to achieve near-optimal performance with significantly lower computational costs than traditional methods. However, current GNN-based approaches typically depend on a central server for training and inference, creating a single point of failure and restricting deployment to specific environments. This paper introduces a novel framework for decentralized inference of GNNs in wireless systems, enabling devices to perform inference without relying on a central server. We validate this framework by applying it to a wireless network multiple access problem, where devices collaboratively infer the optimal power allocation. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves performance comparable to centralized methods while reducing computational complexity by an order of magnitude. Furthermore, we show that the framework is robust against Byzantine attacks, maintaining high performance even when a significant number of devices are compromised. Finally, we examine the impact of device mobility on the framework's performance. Our findings indicate that while mobility introduces challenges, the framework remains effective in dynamic network conditions. This work paves the way for more flexible and scalable decentralized inference solutions in wireless systems. Homicide rates in Brazil have risen steadily over recent decades, with the state of Goiás experiencing particularly severe increases. This study examines the spatial distribution of homicides in Goiás between 2002 and 2014 by analyzing the evolution of spatial clusters using the Kulldorff spatial scan statistic. The findings indicate that homicides in the state are not randomly distributed but are instead concentrated in specific areas. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that homicide rates in these regions have risen consistently throughout the study period. These results underscore the necessity for targeted public policies aimed at reducing violence in the most affected zones. Additionally, the study highlights the utility of the Kulldorff spatial scan statistic for analyzing the spatial distribution of homicides. Finally, the paper explores the potential for applying this methodology to other types of crimes. The dataset used in this work is accessible at http://www.dados.gov.br/. The source code for the Kulldorff spatial scan statistic employed here can be found at https://github.com/fernandocf/scanstat. Accelerated Stochastic Gradient Descent (ASGD) is a widely adopted optimization method for training machine learning models, particularly in deep learning contexts. However, its convergence behavior is heavily influenced by the specific problem characteristics and the level of stochastic noise present. This study examines ASGD's convergence across various scenarios, specifically analyzing how stochastic noise impacts its performance. We demonstrate that ASGD can fail to converge in the presence of significant stochastic noise. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel, model-free, adaptive algorithm designed to ensure convergence regardless of the noise level. Furthermore, we propose a new adaptive approach that achieves faster convergence rates for both strongly convex and non-convex problems. These proposed methods are model-free, requiring no prior knowledge of problem parameters, and are model-adaptive, meaning they automatically adjust to the specific problem being optimized. We validate the effectiveness of these methods through numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results indicate that our adaptive algorithms outperform ASGD in terms of convergence speed and final solution quality. Dexterous manipulation is a critical dexterous robotic task that demands a deep comprehension of object geometry and spatial relationships. Grasping, a fundamental component of dexterous manipulation, has been widely researched, yet existing real-world datasets are limited by the narrow range of object shapes, grasp configurations, and environmental contexts. To address this, we introduce DexGraspNet, a large-scale, diverse, and realistic synthetic dexterous grasp dataset. This resource comprises 1.2 million high-fidelity, real-time rendered images of objects from 100 distinct categories, featuring 100,000 unique objects and 10,000 unique grasp poses. Each grasp configuration includes 3D object geometry, camera parameters, and 3D hand geometry. We validate the efficacy of DexGraspNet by training a dexterous robotic hand to learn a generalizable policy for grasping unseen objects, achieving a success rate of 80.2% on 100 novel object categories. This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-corrected 4D (3D plus respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) sequence designed for body imaging. The approach employs a retrospective, data-driven method to reconstruct motion-corrected 4D volumes from free-breathing acquisitions. Specifically, the 4D data is decomposed into respiratory phases, and each phase is further segmented into respiratory states. A deep convolutional neural network (CNN) is utilized to synthesize motion-corrected 4D volumes by learning the mapping from these respiratory states to the corresponding volumes. The proposed sequence and reconstruction pipeline were evaluated using both phantom and in vivo data. Results demonstrate that the method effectively corrects respiratory motion, yielding high-quality 4D volumes with superior image contrast and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compared to conventional techniques. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness against motion artifacts, even when applied to data acquired with a reduced number of excitations. These findings indicate that the proposed approach holds significant potential for enhancing the efficiency of 4D T2-weighted TSE MRI in clinical settings. InDistill employs a new Information Flow Graph (IFG) to represent the internal data propagation within a DNN. This graph is used to identify and extract the most critical information flow from the source model, which is then integrated into the target model to maintain the original flow characteristics. This paper establishes the topological similarity of non-constant submersion functions within an open subset of the plane, specifically when the level sets are either lines or smooth curves that are asymptotic to lines at infinity. This result extends the well-known theorem regarding the topological similarity of linear functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the topological equivalence of the foliations generated by these submersion functions, generalizing the equivalence of shears and parallel lines. Our approach relies on the concept of topological equivalence for planar foliations, which we define and examine in this work. Additionally, we provide a topological classification of such foliations based on their singularities and the behavior of their leaves at infinity. We also present a method for constructing a topological equivalence between two foliations, contingent upon the classification of their local and global elements. Finally, we explore the relationship between the topological equivalence of planar foliations and the conjugacy of their holonomy groups at hyperbolic singularities. As an application, we derive the topological normal form for hyperbolic singularities of submersion functions in the plane. The study of topological equivalence for planar foliations is motivated by the need to classify these structures, a topic that has garnered significant attention in recent years. We address this problem by examining the local and global characteristics of the foliations, including their singularities, asymptotic lines, and limit cycles. Our findings are supported by illustrative examples and visualizations. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the necessary background on topological equivalence of planar foliations, while Section 3 introduces the topological classification of such foliations. Section 4 presents the main results, and Section 5 applies these findings to the topological classification of hyperbolic singularities for submersion functions in the plane. This study examines a dry-land vegetation model incorporating a non-local grazing term, where the functional response depends on the average plant density across the entire domain. We establish the existence and uniqueness of steady-state solutions and analyze their stability. Furthermore, we explore the phenomenon of grazing-induced pattern formation, demonstrating that these non-local patterns can emerge even when linear stability analysis predicts uniform states. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through numerical simulations. The results indicate that non-local grazing can trigger Turing-type pattern formation, alter the stability of steady states, and generate complex dynamics, including periodic and chaotic oscillations. Additionally, the study reveals the existence of grazing-induced bistability, where both uniform and patterned states coexist. These findings underscore the critical role of non-local grazing in shaping vegetation dynamics and highlight the necessity of accounting for this factor in ecological modeling. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings for ecological theory and future research directions. CountSketch is a widely used streaming algorithm designed to estimate the number of distinct elements in a stream. Although prior research has demonstrated that CountSketch achieves a constant approximation ratio for such estimates, it remains vulnerable to adaptive adversaries. In this work, we present the first rigorous analysis of CountSketch's resilience against adaptive inputs. Our findings indicate that the algorithm maintains a constant approximation ratio when the adversary is allowed to adaptively select only a limited number of items. Furthermore, we establish a matching lower bound, proving that the adversary can reduce the approximation ratio to $O(\log n)$ if permitted to adaptively choose an additional item. Finally, we extend our analysis to the distinct element estimation problem under the adaptive semi-streaming model, demonstrating that CountSketch achieves a constant approximation ratio in this context. Additionally, we provide a lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$ for any algorithm operating under the same constraints. To our knowledge, this represents the first analysis of any streaming algorithm for distinct element estimation within the adaptive semi-streaming model. Our proof relies on a novel application of the "birthday paradox" concept.
