This study examines a secure multi-user wireless system utilizing a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) to enhance physical layer security against eavesdropping, while accounting for hardware impairments (HWI) within the RIS. The RIS is configured to maximize the minimum secure rate across all users. To address HWI, the problem is transformed into a convex form through the introduction of slack variables and the application of the first-order Taylor expansion. Furthermore, a low-complexity alternating optimization algorithm is developed to efficiently solve the resulting convex problem. Numerical simulations are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves the minimum secure rate compared to existing schemes, even under the influence of HWI. Additionally, the computational complexity of the proposed algorithm is substantially lower than that of other methods. Finally, the impact of HWI on the system's secure performance is analyzed. Simulation outcomes indicate that the proposed scheme remains effective in mitigating HWI effects, thereby achieving a higher minimum secure rate. Moreover, the proposed algorithm exhibits superior performance relative to other schemes in terms of minimum secure rate, even when HWI is present. We propose treating executive function as a contrastive value strategy, where the goal is to maximize the difference between the value of the current perception and that of a randomly sampled one. This paper investigates noncommutative countable principal bundles within the context of locally compact Hausdorff spaces and their C*-algebras. We demonstrate that a specific class of C*-algebra actions by discrete groups, characterized by the existence of continuous approximate identities for their fixed-point subalgebras, corresponds to the notion of a locally trivial bundle. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which a continuous action of a locally compact Hausdorff space on a C*-algebra, where the space acts through abelian locally compact groups, qualifies as a principal bundle. Additionally, we provide a characterization of actions that constitute countable principal bundles using the concept of continuous bundle of C*-algebras. Finally, we examine the relationship between these countable principal bundles and their associated continuous bundle of C*-algebras. As an application, we present a characterization of continuous bundles of C*-algebras based on their local sections. Many results in this work extend to continuous actions of locally compact Hausdorff spaces on C*-algebras that are not necessarily unital. In the final section, we explore the connection between continuous actions forming principal bundles and those inducing continuous bundles of C*-algebras, with a specific focus on the case where the acting space is a compact group. We demonstrate that when the acting space is the circle group, the associated continuous bundle of C*-algebras is necessarily unital. We also address the challenge of constructing a continuous bundle of C*-algebras from an arbitrary continuous action of a compact group. Finally, we establish that if the action of a compact group is free, the resulting continuous bundle of C*-algebras is locally trivial. This finding generalizes a result by J. Dixmier regarding continuous actions of compact Lie groups on unital C*-algebras. The methods employed in this work are applicable to the broader context of continuous actions of locally compact Hausdorff spaces on unital C*-algebras. We illustrate this by providing an example of a continuous action of a compact group on a unital C*-algebra that does not yield a continuous bundle of unital C*-algebras. This example also serves to show that the continuous bundle of C*-algebras associated with a continuous action of a compact group is not necessarily unital. The paper concludes with an open question. This study examines the optical response of a $q$-deformed optomechanical system featuring two optical cavities coupled to a single mechanical oscillator. We analyze how the $q$-deformation parameter influences the refractive index, dispersion, and group velocity of the system. Our results indicate that the $q$-deformation can induce fast and slow light effects, with the speed of light reaching zero at specific mechanical resonances. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the $q$-deformation can simultaneously achieve high clarity and enhanced light speed in both fast and slow light regimes. These findings offer valuable insights for the development of all-optical devices. Additionally, we explore the potential for generating nonclassical states, including Schrödinger cat states, within the mechanical oscillator. Finally, we show that the $q$-deformation can suppress the decay of the mechanical oscillator's coherence. These outcomes suggest that $q$-deformation may serve as a valuable tool for advancing quantum optomechanics. This study examines the Two-Rotors Model featuring two adjacent rotors with opposite moments of inertia, a configuration that mimics R-parity violating scenarios in Beyond the Standard Model physics. We identify two distinct scissors modes, both exhibiting adverse frequency behavior relative to the rotors' moments of inertia. The first mode arises from the relative rotation of both rotors, while the second results from the relative rotation of one rotor against the center of mass of the combined system. We analyze the conditions under which these modes become unstable and explore their potential implications for R-parity violation. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of a friction term on the rotors' dynamics. Finally, we establish a correspondence between the classical and quantum descriptions of this model. Our findings suggest that the system's behavior is governed by a single parameter, defined as the ratio of the rotors' moments of inertia. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model can be solved exactly in the quantum regime. These results may prove valuable for describing R-parity violating phenomena in Beyond the Standard Model physics. The paper concludes with a discussion of the model's applications. The Unruh effect, which describes how a uniformly accelerated observer perceives a thermal bath of particles despite a vacuum state for inertial observers, has been extensively researched. This study demonstrates that the future and past light cones of an accelerated observer become entangled, resulting in a non-zero entanglement entropy. This phenomenon is interpreted as a manifestation of the Unruh effect within the entanglement structure of light cones. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the Unruh phenomenon can be detected through the Berry phase of the accelerated observer. This approach offers a novel method for identifying the Unruh phenomenon, one that avoids the need for particle detectors. Additionally, the findings suggest that the Unruh phenomenon is not restricted to timelike acceleration; it also occurs in the context of light cones for null acceleration. These results provide a new perspective on the relationship between entanglement entropy and the Unruh effect, while also opening avenues for future experimental verification. Finally, the study explores the implications of these findings for the black hole information paradox. The paper concludes with a discussion of the limitations of this approach. This paper examines global vector bundles on a complex manifold $X$ through the lens of their characteristic forms. We establish novel positivity criteria for globally defined vector bundles by utilizing positivity conditions on their associated characteristic forms. Furthermore, we derive new push-forward formulae for globally defined vector bundles under holomorphic submersions. As an application, we present a novel approach to proving the openness of the positivity cone for globally defined vector bundles. Additionally, we apply these findings to investigate the openness of the nef cone for line bundles within the context of K\"ahler spaces. Finally, we explore global vector bundles on K\"ahler spaces as a means to extend established results from complex manifolds to K\"ahler spaces. Notably, we demonstrate that the openness of the nef cone for line bundles does not necessarily hold for general K\"ahler spaces. The paper concludes with an exploration of global vector bundles on singular spaces. Specifically, we examine global vector bundles on singular projective varieties and global reflexive vector bundles on K\"ahler spaces. We illustrate that the openness of the nef cone for line bundles fails in general for both singular projective varieties and K\"ahler spaces. Moreover, we show that the openness of the nef cone for line bundles on projective varieties remains an unresolved issue. Finally, we provide an example of a K\"ahler space admitting no global vector bundles. These findings suggest that global vector bundles on K\"ahler spaces represent a distinct and significant area of study. We investigate the post-merger dynamics of a binary neutron star system featuring a magnetized neutrino-cooled accretion disk, utilizing a new general-relativistic hydrodynamics code that integrates magnetic fields, neutrino leakage, and rotation. Our simulations reveal that the disk's evolution is primarily driven by neutrino emission and magnetic field dissipation. The energy released via neutrinos is sufficient to generate a significant outflow, with a mass of approximately $10^{-3} M_{\odot}$ ejected at velocities around $0.1c$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnetic field amplifies within the outflow, reaching strengths of roughly $10^{15}$ G at the disk surface. This amplified field is critical for powering a central engine, such as a magnetar, which can subsequently drive a late-time electromagnetic transient. Additionally, we find that the outflow's angular momentum is low, resulting in a low accretion rate onto the central object. Consequently, the outflow remains optically thick to electron scattering, and the magnetic field is too weak to significantly influence the dynamics of the optically thick region. Finally, we show that the outflow's composition is dominated by electron-positron pairs, with a baryon mass fraction of approximately $10^{-2}$. These findings indicate that the outflow is likely a mixture of baryonic and pair components, a scenario that could explain the observed properties of short gamma-ray bursts. Overall, our results suggest that neutrino-driven outflows from magnetized accretion disks can produce a substantial amount of ejecta, potentially accounting for the mass of the disk and the characteristics of short gamma-ray bursts. We conducted a systematic investigation into the tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies (ETGs) within the HSC-SSP Wide Survey, utilizing a newly developed automated detection algorithm. This method identifies tidal features in both the outer and inner regions of galaxies, quantifying their flux relative to the host galaxy. Our analysis reveals that the flux fraction of outer features scales with stellar mass, whereas inner features show no such correlation. Furthermore, we observed that the flux fraction of outer features is higher in galaxies with lower stellar velocity dispersion ($\sigma_{\rm{V}}$) and those exhibiting larger effective radii ($r_{\rm{e}}$). These findings suggest that the outer features are primarily composed of tidal debris from past mergers, while inner features likely arise from dynamical processes such as bar instabilities. Additionally, we estimated the merger rate for ETGs with $\sigma_{\rm{V}} < 150$ km/s by analyzing the fraction of galaxies possessing outer features. This study extends the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), introduced in the first paper of this series, to address the formation of bipolar outflows in protostars and galaxies. The gravitational field is modeled as a superposition of monopole and dipole components, where the dipole term generates a repulsive force. This repulsion drives the formation of bipolar outflows in protostars, while the dipole field in galaxies is hypothesized to originate from dark matter. The analysis demonstrates that the monopole-dipole superposition creates a specific region where the attractive monopole force dominates, thereby restricting the outflow to a confined area. Furthermore, the theory indicates that the dipole field can be either attractive or repulsive depending on the azimuthal angle. Consequently, the resulting outflow velocity varies with this angle, producing a bipolar structure characterized by a central star or galaxy core surrounded by two opposing outflowing regions. This phenomenon is observed in protostars as Herbig-Haro objects and in galaxies as bipolar radio jets. The paper also examines the stability of this bipolar configuration and the conditions required for its formation. Additionally, the theory offers a novel explanation for the rotation curves of galaxies. Finally, the study explores the potential for bipolar outflows to generate magnetic fields and the associated energy dissipation. The proposed model is validated by comparing its predictions with observational data. Ultimately, the research concludes that the bipolar outflow phenomenon is a result of a repellent gravitational effect. Keywords: Gravity, Galaxy, Protostar, Outflow, Rotation curve. We conducted a targeted search for optical counterparts to fast radio bursts (FRBs) using the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF). This search covered 12 FRBs identified by the Parkes Multi-beam Radio Telescope (PMRT) with well-determined positions and known redshifts. Our analysis included both simultaneous and delayed optical emission, with a specific focus on the optical afterglow of FRB 20121127A. We established a 95% confidence upper limit on the optical fluence of $1.1 \times 10^{-10}$ erg cm$^{-2}$ for the afterglow of FRB 20121127A, which is 100 times lower than the fluence of its radio burst. Additionally, we set simultaneous fluence upper limits ranging from $1.1 \times 10^{-10}$ to $1.1 \times 10^{-8}$ erg cm$^{-2}$ for the remaining 11 FRBs. These results indicate that if optical emission is present, it must be extremely faint, occurring at a rate at least 100 times lower than that of the radio emission. This finding constrains models predicting a common radio-optical emission mechanism and suggests that any optical emission is likely produced by a distinct process. Furthermore, we conducted a blind search for optical transients coincident with 1,000 FRBs lacking known positions, finding no significant optical emission. This absence of a population of bright, simultaneous optical transients suggests that the optical emission from FRBs is not driven by a mechanism capable of producing a large number of bright events. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the nature of FRBs. The data are available at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stad1000. This study examines the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ decay process, where $n=1,2,3$, by analyzing the hadronic loop mechanism. Finally, the paper explores the potential for discovering new exotic hadrons through the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ channel. Bayesian Nested Sampling (BNS) is a powerful method for estimating the evidence of a model, which serves as a basis for model comparison. However, BNS is computationally intensive, and its performance is highly sensitive to the choice of step selector. This study evaluates various step selectors, including those based on Gaussian processes, to identify the most efficient options. Our findings indicate that model-based approaches, particularly those utilizing Gaussian processes, yield the best results. We demonstrate that these methods significantly reduce the number of live points required to achieve a specific evidence accuracy, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. Additionally, we examine the impact of different prior distributions on model-based selectors and explore the relationship between the number of live points and the posterior distribution of the evidence. Finally, we apply these optimized step selectors to a cosmological model comparison scenario. The results confirm that these methods substantially improve BNS performance, reducing the required live points by a factor of 2 to 3.5 compared to standard approaches. This reduction translates to a 4 to 10-fold decrease in computational time. The code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/mauricio-ramos/BNS_step_selector. Distance labeling for graphs assigns short labels to vertices such that the pairwise distance between any two vertices can be determined solely from their labels. While this concept was introduced over a decade ago, the most efficient labels for planar graphs to date have a length of $O(\log^2 n)$. This paper presents the first fault-resilient distance labeling scheme for planar graphs, capable of tolerating a constant number of vertex failures. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any planar graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, there exists a labeling scheme where each label has a length of $O(\log^3 n)$. Furthermore, this scheme remains functional even if a constant number of vertices are removed. Additionally, we provide a nearly tight upper bound for fault-resilient distance labeling in general graphs, showing that $O(\log^3 n)$ labels suffice to handle the failure of a constant number of vertices. This result improves upon the previous best bound of $O(\log^4 n)$ established by Berman et al. (2019). Finally, we extend our findings to graphs of bounded genus, achieving $O(\log^3 n)$ labels for planar graphs and $O(\log^3 n + g \log^2 n)$ labels for graphs with genus $g$. In both the planar and bounded genus scenarios, the labels are fault-resilient against the failure of a constant number of vertices. All results in this paper are derived from a unified approach. We also explore extensions of our labeling schemes to handle edge failures and discuss potential avenues for future research.

Keywords: Distance labeling, planar graphs, genus, fault-resilience.

This study examines two-particle correlations within a dissipative Bose-Hubbard model subjected to an external driving force. The system is analyzed using both time-domain and frequency-domain correlation functions. In the frequency domain, the correlation function is defined as the Fourier transform of the time-domain version. The investigation covers two distinct correlation types: one involving two bosons at the same site and another involving bosons at neighboring sites. Results indicate that the frequency-domain correlation function for on-site bosons exhibits a Lorentzian profile, whereas the function for nearest-neighbor bosons displays a Gaussian profile. This paper establishes the solvability of elliptic equations in divergence form within $L^2$, where the coefficients are represented as currents. Specifically, we demonstrate $L^p$-estimates for the gradient of the solution and its associated Riesz potential. These findings extend the work of Fabes, Jenkins, and Sario, who previously addressed the case of functions. Furthermore, our results generalize the findings of Fabes and Stroock regarding elliptic equations with rough coefficients. As an application, we prove the solvability of the $\bar{\partial}$-equation for $(0,1)$-currents on the Heisenberg group. Additionally, we show that the Fabes-Jenkins-Sario estimates apply to the Riesz potentials of $(0,1)$-currents on the polydisc. Finally, we provide an example of a current that fails to be the potential of any other current. This study addresses the challenge of identifying out-of-distribution (OOD) data within Gaussian process (GP) regression. We introduce a novel method that partitions the input space into multiple strata, where each stratum is defined by a distinct mean function. This approach is grounded in the concept of distributional GPs, which model the distribution of function values rather than the values themselves. By employing a distributional GP to represent the mean function, we can identify the specific stratum to which a new data point belongs. Our findings demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques for OOD detection. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the method's convergence rate. This study examines a driven, open optical-lattice system featuring a Floquet-heating mechanism. We demonstrate that this system can sustain a Bose condensation within a scar-like state, a phenomenon that defies the standard expectation that heating invariably disrupts such condensations. This heating-induced Bose condensation is realized through a specific balance between heating and particle loss, a condition that can be precisely controlled by adjusting the driving and loss rates. Furthermore, we find that the system's relaxation dynamics are governed by the decay of a single mode, which corresponds to the stationary scar-like state. This mode exhibits a non-Gaussian probability distribution, a characteristic typically associated with chaotic systems. Our findings offer a novel approach to achieving heating-induced Bose condensation in open quantum systems and provide a new method for generating scar-like states. Additionally, this work establishes a new framework for investigating the interplay between heating and dissipation in open quantum systems. Finally, we explore the potential applications of this heating-induced Bose condensation in the context of quantum information processing. These applications are enabled by the unique properties of the scar-like state, including its long lifetime, non-Gaussian probability distribution, and the ease with which its parameters can be tuned. We anticipate that this research will inspire further investigations into heating-induced Bose condensation and its applications in quantum information processing. Our work also highlights the potential for using open quantum systems to explore the complex interplay between heating and dissipation. This study establishes an enhanced Alexandrov maximum principle for the Monge–Ampère equation with a bounded right-hand side, thereby proving uniform Hölder continuity for the corresponding solutions. The methodology relies on a novel technique involving the analysis of the geometry of level sets of the solution. As a result, we demonstrate that the modulus of Hölder continuity for these solutions is optimal. Furthermore, this approach yields a new Alexandrov maximum principle applicable to the Monge–Ampère equation within unbounded domains. Finally, we examine the Alexandrov–Bak–Pensser example, which illustrates a solution exhibiting linear Hölder continuity in an unbounded domain. Additionally, we present a counterexample to a conjecture proposed by Caffarelli, Nirenberg, and J. Spruck. Finally, we extend our findings to the complex setting, deriving an enhanced maximum principle for the complex Monge–Ampère equation and establishing the uniform Hölder continuity of its solutions. We introduce a statistical framework for analyzing time-domain data from non-periodic optical clocks, which are currently under development. This approach is applicable to any system where timing data is recorded at irregular intervals. We demonstrate that the Allan variance remains a valid metric for characterizing the stability of such clocks. Furthermore, we derive the analytical form of the Allan variance for non-periodic clocks, revealing that it converges to the standard periodic clock expression as the sampling rate increases. Finally, we validate this analytical model using a numerical simulation of an optical clock. This work provides a foundation for the time-domain analysis of future optical clocks and other systems generating data at irregular sampling rates. This study introduces a joint failure restoration, fault prevention, and energy-efficient resource management framework designed for Software-Defined Networking (SDN) within Service Function Chaining (SFC) in fog-supported environments. The primary objective is to minimize total energy consumption by dynamically adjusting the number of active switches based on current network demand. Furthermore, the proposed scheme aims to reduce the end-to-end delay of service requests by optimizing the placement of service functions. To achieve this, a centralized controller is developed to simultaneously prevent faults and restore network failures. This approach enables the controller to jointly optimize the scheduling of service functions and the configuration of network resources. Additionally, the method incorporates a fault prevention mechanism that allows the controller to proactively identify and mitigate potential network failures. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme effectively reduces energy usage and enhances the timeliness of service requests. Finally, the scheme's ability to prevent faults and restore failures is validated through simulations involving network failures. The paper concludes with a discussion on the simulation outcomes. The choice of loss function is a critical component of deep learning model design, yet its specific impact on model behavior remains poorly understood. This study investigates how various loss functions influence the behavior of models trained with gradient surgery, a technique that restricts the magnitude of gradient updates. Our findings indicate that gradient surgery can alter the relative effectiveness of different loss functions. Specifically, when combined with gradient surgery, the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss yields superior results compared to mean squared error (MSE) in the task of training a classifier to distinguish between models trained on real data versus those trained on synthetic data generated by a generative model. This outcome contrasts with standard gradient descent training, where MSE typically outperforms KL divergence in this context. We attribute this improvement to gradient surgery's ability to prevent the model from overfitting to the synthetic data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that gradient surgery can be effectively applied to large-scale language modeling, achieving performance comparable to full-precision training while utilizing only a fraction of the computational resources. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the development of generative models. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/gradient-surgery. Holographic error correction codes are defined by their linear distance scaling and efficient encoding circuits. While most existing codes rely on constant or polynomial distance scaling, we introduce a novel class of codes that achieve linear distance scaling while maintaining constant depth encoding circuits. Our construction utilizes a modified Multi-scale Entanglement Renormalization Ansatz (MERA) that incorporates power-law dependencies. We demonstrate that these codes can correct any error affecting a constant number of physical qubits, provided the error is localized within a region of constant diameter. Furthermore, we establish that the code distance scales linearly with the system size. We also examine the relationship between our codes and the hypergraph states proposed by Brown et al. (2020), which are known to have linear distance. Finally, we outline a method to construct a family of quantum LDPC codes with constant rate and linear distance by concatenating our codes with a classical LDPC code. This approach yields a family of quantum LDPC codes featuring linear distance, constant rate, and constant locality. Additionally, we show that these codes can be implemented using a constant number of qubits per gate. Our findings suggest that holographic codes can be engineered to exhibit power-law dependencies, thereby enhancing their fault-tolerance capabilities. This paper addresses the Optimal Conservation Voltage Decrease (OCVD) challenge within Integrated Primary-Secondary Distribution Systems (IPSDS), where voltage reduction is utilized to lower energy losses and defer infrastructure upgrades. The proposed approach employs a distributed optimization framework that utilizes distributed Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to solve the OCVD problem. This method ensures that distribution companies (DisCos) do not need to exchange sensitive operational data, such as network topology and load profiles, with the aggregator managing the IPSDS. The study validates the proposed solution through simulations on a real-world IPSDS, comparing its performance against a centralized optimization approach. Results demonstrate that the distributed method achieves performance comparable to the centralized solution while significantly reducing communication overhead. Furthermore, the paper provides a theoretical analysis of the proposed solution, proving that it converges to the optimal solution of the OCVD problem. This paper investigates a nonstochastic bandit framework where an advisor, rather than the learner, selects arms. Each arm incurs a specific delay, and the advisor is penalized for the cumulative delay of all chosen arms. We introduce a novel model featuring arm-dependent delays and establish a minimax lower bound for the expected total delay of the advisor. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm that matches this lower bound up to a constant factor, thereby resolving an open question posed by Bubeck et al. (2021). Additionally, we examine a variant where the advisor's delay is unknown and must be learned, demonstrating that the same regret bound applies. Finally, we explore a further extension in which the advisor's delay is a function of both the selected arm and the current time. In this scenario, we derive a regret lower bound that scales with the square of the time horizon, and we present an algorithm that achieves this bound up to a constant factor. This result improves upon the best existing algorithm for a related problem by a factor of $\sqrt{T}$. Our findings are supported by numerical experiments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Ankit-1234/Nonstochastic_Bandits_and_Advisors_with_Arm-Dependent_Delays.

This paper introduces LEATHER, a framework designed to generate human-like text in dialogue. We begin by analyzing the linguistic characteristics of human conversation, specifically examining the distribution of sentence lengths and the frequency of various sentence types. Subsequently, we develop a method to learn these sentence-level traits from a given prompt. Finally, we demonstrate that LEATHER can produce high-quality responses that closely resemble human utterances. Our experimental results indicate that the system's output is indistinguishable from human responses in 30% of cases, compared to 10% for the baseline. Additionally, we show that LEATHER can be adapted to mimic the stylistic features of specific individuals. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhi-1999/LEATHER. Our findings suggest that LEATHER holds significant potential for applications requiring human-like communication, such as chatbots and virtual assistants. We also explore the ethical implications of our work, particularly the risk of creating deceptive AI agents that may mislead users into believing they are interacting with humans. This study introduces a novel surrogate modeling approach utilizing a sequence of Gaussian processes to estimate stress distributions along an offshore wind turbine's structure. The method is validated using a high-fidelity finite element model of an existing turbine, where stress data from the blade, tower, and transition piece are generated via a Monte Carlo simulation of 100,000 scenarios. These scenarios vary key operational and environmental parameters, including wind speed, wind direction, rotor speed, and wave height. The proposed chained Gaussian process model is benchmarked against a standard Gaussian process and a Gaussian process regression tree. Results indicate that the chained model achieves superior accuracy compared to both alternatives, demonstrating a 10% reduction in mean squared error relative to the standard Gaussian process and a 20% reduction compared to the regression tree. Furthermore, the chained model exhibits greater robustness to hyperparameter selection than the standard Gaussian process. Finally, the model's ability to capture stress distribution patterns across the structure is confirmed through the analysis of estimated stress quantiles. This methodology offers a promising avenue for future probabilistic structural analysis of wind turbines. This paper investigates the $R_\infty$ property within the $\infty$-limit of nilpotent quotients for specific classes of generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups. We demonstrate that for a broad category of these groups, the property holds true in the $\infty$-limit. Furthermore, we establish that the property fails for certain groups where the underlying directed graph is bipartite. Finally, we present several open questions regarding this research area. Additionally, we offer a concise proof of the $R_\infty$ property for nilpotent quotients of abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups, as noted in [J. Algebra 503 (2018) 120--140]. This approach relies on the theory of linear monodromy and extends the methodology used by the first author in [J. Algebra 503 (2018) 120--140]. This study introduces a new framework for reconstructing time-resolved data, such as images or spectra, from noisy, time-dependent measurements. This paper introduces SceNDD, a situation-based naturalistic driving dataset designed to facilitate research on autonomous vehicle decision-making. Comprising 1,000 driving episodes, each lasting 10 to 20 seconds, the data was gathered using a mobile sensor suite. The dataset features 14 sensor modalities, including 10 high-frequency streams at 100 Hz (such as LiDAR, cameras, and IMU) and four low-frequency streams (such as GPS and OBD). We provide a detailed description of the data collection methodology and offer a comprehensive analysis of the recordings, covering data quality, sensor characteristics, and driving scenarios. Furthermore, we present a novel, open-source data processing pipeline that enables users to access the raw data and extract specific features. Finally, we demonstrate the dataset's utility by applying a reinforcement learning algorithm to solve a specific decision-making task. The entire dataset and processing pipeline are publicly available at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/SceNDD. This resource is intended to support the development of data-driven decision-making models for autonomous vehicles. Additionally, we hope it will serve as a benchmark for evaluating new learning-based approaches in the field of autonomous driving. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 details the data collection process; Section 4 presents the data analysis; and Section 5 illustrates the application of the dataset to autonomous driving decision-making. The paper concludes with a discussion of the dataset's limitations and potential future directions. This study examines the exclusive production of $J/\psi+\eta_c$ and $J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) at a center-of-mass energy of approximately 10.6 GeV. By employing the color-singlet model alongside next-to-leading-order QCD corrections, we analyze the angular distributions of the $J/\psi$ vector meson. Our calculations incorporate both the polarization of the initial $e^+e^-$ beams and the spin of the $\eta_c$ or $\chi_{cJ}$ mesons. We present the theoretical predictions for the corresponding differential cross sections. Furthermore, we compare our results with existing experimental data from the BESIII collaboration. Finally, we explore the potential for measuring these processes at the upcoming BEPCII facility. Our findings indicate that the $J/\psi+\eta_c$ channel offers the most favorable prospects for investigation, with a predicted cross section of roughly 1.2 fb. Additionally, the angular distributions of the $J/\psi$ in this channel are highly sensitive to the polarization of the $\eta_c$ meson. In contrast, the $J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$ channels are expected to be significantly more challenging to measure due to their lower cross sections. However, the $J/\psi$ angular distributions in these channels exhibit distinct features that can be used to determine the polarization of the $\chi_{cJ}$ mesons. Specifically, the $J/\psi$ angular distribution in the $J/\psi+\chi_{c2}$ channel is particularly sensitive to the polarization of the $\chi_{c2}$ meson. Our analysis suggests that the BEPCII collider is well-suited for investigating these exclusive processes. This study examines how Signal users perceive and comprehend the app's PINs. Through a survey of 1,000 Signal users, we discovered that 40% lack a clear understanding of what a PIN is, 25% believe it serves no purpose, and 10% are unaware that Signal even utilizes PINs. Furthermore, we identified that users who do understand PINs often hold incorrect beliefs regarding their function, such as thinking they are required for account creation or that they are the sole method for account recovery. These findings highlight a significant gap between Signal's intended security mechanisms and user comprehension, suggesting that this disconnect could undermine the app's security model. To address this, we propose a redesign of Signal's PIN system aimed at enhancing user understanding and usability. We validated this redesign by demonstrating that it improves users' ability to correctly identify PIN usage scenarios and successfully recover their accounts. Additionally, we conducted a qualitative analysis of 100 in-depth interviews with Signal users to explore their broader perceptions of the app's security features. Our analysis revealed that users are generally satisfied with Signal's security, yet they also expressed concerns about the app's privacy practices and the potential risks associated with end-to-end encryption. These insights offer valuable direction for Signal's future security and privacy initiatives. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of our findings and recommendations for enhancing Signal's security and privacy. Solar irradiance, which varies with the sun's position, is a critical factor in modeling the energy systems of buildings and communities. This paper introduces a new numerical integration technique called solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature (SWGQ), designed to efficiently and accurately compute time-integrated quantities under solar irradiance. By deriving SWGQ from the classical Gaussian quadrature, we ensure that it maintains the same high-order accuracy. The method's order of accuracy is validated through numerical experiments, and its effectiveness is demonstrated by calculating the time-integrated temperature of a building's interior. These results confirm that SWGQ is both precise and efficient for integrating functions weighted by solar irradiance. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to any solar irradiance model, including the widely used Perez model. Consequently, SWGQ offers a valuable tool for modeling the energy dynamics of buildings and communities. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leeyu123456/SWGQ. We demonstrate that for any arithmetic group of uniform type, the growth rate of its nontrivial conjugacy classes is bounded by the group's virtual cohomological dimension. This finding confirms a conjecture proposed by Harborth and Harer. Furthermore, we establish that within the class of arithmetic groups of uniform type, stiffness is bounded precisely when charmability is bounded. Additionally, we provide a characterization of boundedness for both properties in terms of the rank of the fundamental group of the corresponding hyperbolic 3-manifolds. Finally, we present an example of an arithmetic group that is neither charmable nor stiff. Our results rely on the recently proven finiteness of the rank of the fundamental group for hyperbolic 3-manifolds with small volume. We also offer a new, self-contained proof of this finiteness specifically for volumes less than 3.0. This proof utilizes the recently established bound on the systole of hyperbolic 3-manifolds with a fixed number of cusps, which is derived from the theory of modular forms. Moreover, we show that this bound on the systole is optimal. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential extensions of these findings to broader classes of arithmetic groups. Position estimation for known categories is a fundamental task in computer vision, yet existing methods are restricted to trained categories, thereby limiting their utility in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a zero-shot approach to position estimation that operates without requiring training or validation data from the target categories. Our method utilizes a pre-trained vision-language model to derive category-specific descriptors, which are then employed to estimate object positions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on two key tasks: 1) position estimation for multiple object categories within a single image, and 2) position estimation for a specific object category across numerous images. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both scenarios. Furthermore, we show that the method is robust to variations in the pre-trained vision-language model and can be effectively applied to both 2D and 3D position estimation. This study introduces MAPPIES, a novel Monte-Carlo code designed to simulate the production of ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray photons via inverse external-Compton scattering (IC) of polarized photons originating from the accretion disk around blazar supermassive black holes. The code incorporates a realistic accretion disk model and accounts for the polarization of the seed photon field. We apply MAPPIES to analyze the UV/soft X-ray excess observed in the spectra of blazars, specifically the Flat Spectrum Radio Quasar (FSRQ) 3C 273 and the BL Lacertae object Mrk 421. Our results indicate that the polarization degree of the accretion disk's seed photon field is approximately 10% for 3C 273 and 20% for Mrk 421. Furthermore, the polarization angle of the seed photon field is determined to be roughly 10 degrees for 3C 273 and 80 degrees for Mrk 421. These findings suggest that the accretion disk is a viable source of UV/soft X-ray emission in these blazars. Additionally, we demonstrate that the polarization angle of the accretion disk can be estimated by comparing the polarization angle of the X-ray excess with that of the optical continuum. Finally, we show that the polarization degree of the accretion disk can be derived from the ratio of the optical polarization degree to the polarization degree of the optical continuum. These results offer valuable insights for interpreting the polarization properties of blazar accretion disks. The MAPPIES code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/MAPPIES. We examine the analytic extension of complex landscapes, defined as the collection of all possible minima for a given potential. We demonstrate that for polynomial potentials, the analytic extension of the landscape comprises a finite union of algebraic hypersurfaces within the space of complex parameters. Furthermore, we establish that the derivative of the landscape's extension is meromorphic, and we provide an algorithm to calculate its extension. These findings are applicable to any potential, regardless of its physical origin. As a specific application, we analyze the analytic extension of the landscape in the MSSM, focusing on the parameter space where the lightest Higgs boson mass equals 125 GeV. We also present a numerical algorithm to compute the derivative of this extension and apply it to the MSSM scenario. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the study of complex landscapes. This study investigates the quantized fragmentation of a QCD string featuring helical color fields, focusing on baryon production. By employing the Lund model, we simulate string breaking and meson formation. To achieve baryon creation, we introduce a quark-antiquark pair into the meson, resulting in a quark-diquark configuration. We analyze the mass distribution of these quark-diquark states and compare our findings with experimental data. The results indicate that the model successfully reproduces the observed baryon mass distribution. Small-area estimation (SAE) is a statistical approach used to derive reliable estimates for small populations, such as those within specific geographic regions or demographic groups. This paper reviews the design-based and model-based frameworks underlying SAE, with a specific focus on their application in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). It examines the advantages and constraints of each framework, supported by a case study from Malawi that compares the two methods. The findings indicate that model-based techniques are more readily available and easier to implement than design-based methods; however, model-based approaches demand greater statistical expertise and are more susceptible to violations of model assumptions. Consequently, the study recommends that in LMICs, model-based SAE should be employed when high-quality data are accessible, whereas design-based SAE is preferable when data quality is compromised. Furthermore, the paper outlines the necessary steps for implementing SAE in LMICs and highlights the critical role of capacity building in this endeavor. Finally, it addresses the challenges of integrating SAE into national statistical systems and the need for ongoing monitoring and evaluation. The authors conclude that SAE is a vital tool for generating high-quality small-area estimates in LMICs, offering significant potential to enhance decision-making processes. This work serves as a comprehensive resource for statisticians and policymakers interested in utilizing SAE within the LMIC context. The paper is structured into eight sections: an introduction, a review of SAE methods, a case study, a discussion of implementation challenges, and conclusions, followed by five appendices containing supplementary material. The wagering model, originally proposed by St. Andrew Kelly in 1956, involves a gambler betting on a sequence of independent and identically distributed events. This paper examines a continuous-time variant of the model where the payoff is delivered as a quantum state. We demonstrate that the gambler's optimal betting strategy remains unchanged despite the quantum nature of the payoff. Furthermore, we establish that the resulting wealth evolves as a continuous-time quantum Markov process. Finally, we derive the optimal betting strategy for a scenario where the gambler's payoff is subsequently measured. In this case, the optimal strategy is determined by the classical wagering model, with the betting odds adjusted to reflect the quantum state of the payoff. Additionally, we explore a scenario where the gambler is permitted to bet on the measurement outcomes of the payoff. In this instance, the optimal strategy is derived by solving a semidefinite program. Finally, we illustrate that this approach generalizes the discrete-time model to continuous time. These findings are applicable to quantum gambling scenarios involving quantum payoffs, such as those found in quantum betting markets. Furthermore, the findings of this work can be utilized to investigate the structure of conformal blocks in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. Our proposed phase-locking-free TF-QKD is expected to significantly advance the development of long-distance quantum communication networks. This paper introduces a novel approach for evaluating translator reliability within the translation services industry. The proposed method relies on two key assumptions: first, that a translator's reliability remains constant over time; and second, that reliability can be quantified by the probability of producing a correct translation. These rules are derived by applying the optical theorem to the eigenchannels of the scattering matrix. A key advantage of this approach is that it circumvents the need to calculate the complete scattering matrix. Instead, it relies solely on the partial derivatives of the eigenchannels with respect to the energy of the incident particle. We demonstrate the application of this method to two specific scenarios: the absorption of a scalar particle by a black hole and the absorption of a vector particle by a black hole. In the latter case, we derive the sum rules for the polarization tensor components and apply them to determine the absorption cross section of a vector particle by a Schwarzschild black hole. Furthermore, we examine the sum rules for the absorption cross section of a vector particle by a Reissner-Nordstrom black hole, where we identify an additional contribution arising from the black hole's electric charge. Finally, we discuss the implications of these sum rules for the decay of massive vector particles into black holes. t-SNE is a widely used method for visualizing high-dimensional data by mapping it to a 2D plane. However, it fails to preserve local structures effectively and is unsuitable for spherical data. This approach integrates the von Mises-Fisher distribution with t-SNE, enabling the learning of a low-dimensional representation that maintains local structures while accommodating spherical data characteristics. Furthermore, we show that VMF-SNE surpasses other existing spherical data representation techniques, such as Stiefel-SNE and von Mises SNE. We present diagrammatic Monte Carlo findings on the energy of the Fermi polaron in two dimensions, incorporating both fermion-impurity and fermion-fermion interactions. Our results indicate that the polaron energy is highly sensitive to the strength of the fermion-fermion interaction, a factor that is notably absent in prior studies. Furthermore, we observe that the polaron's effective mass remains nearly constant across the entire range of fermion-fermion interaction strengths. These findings align with recent experimental data from the same system. Additionally, we demonstrate that the polaron energy can be accurately approximated by a simple linear combination of the two interaction strengths. Finally, we compare our diagrammatic Monte Carlo outcomes with those from other theoretical and experimental approaches. Our analysis reveals that the polaron energy is well-described by a linear combination of the two interaction strengths, whereas the effective mass exhibits a more complex dependence on these interactions. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this methodology to investigate the Bose-Einstein condensation of polarons. We introduce a quantum emulation protocol for fermionic systems utilizing a hybrid digital-analog computing approach. This method is specifically designed for fermionic quantum chemistry, enabling the emulation of the fermionic Hamiltonian within a spin-1/2 system. Our analysis demonstrates that the hybrid digital-analog technique offers superior efficiency compared to purely digital methods. Furthermore, we establish that the error in the emulated Hamiltonian scales linearly with the evolution time, a finding that aligns with the principles of first-order Trotterization. Finally, we illustrate the application of this protocol to the hydrogen molecule, showing that it can accurately emulate the system's time evolution. These results indicate that the hybrid digital-analog approach holds significant potential for quantum computing applications. Additionally, our findings suggest that this method is well-suited for implementation on near-term quantum devices. This connection enables the derivation of the Christoffel-Darboux formula for these polynomials using inclusion-exclusion principles. This paper establishes a Hitchin liaison between cubic surfaces and specific Del Pezzo surfaces of degree 5, which arise as Hitchin sections on Veech curve surfaces. We demonstrate that these degree 5 Del Pezzo surfaces possess numerous interesting geometric characteristics, including the existence of many lines, the presence of elliptic fibrations, and the existence of K3 fibrations. Furthermore, we provide an explicit construction of the Hitchin sections for the Veech curve. Finally, we offer a geometric interpretation of the Hitchin sections within the context of the Hitchin fibration. As an application, we construct a nontrivial Hitchin section on the Veech curve that is not isomorphic to any cubic surface. Additionally, we present an explicit example of a Hitchin section on the Veech curve that admits an elliptic fibration. This example is significant because it is neither a cubic surface nor a Del Pezzo surface of degree 5. We also provide an explicit description of the elliptic fibration for this specific section. Finally, we construct a Hitchin section on the Veech curve that features exactly 10 lines. This example is also not a cubic surface or a degree 5 Del Pezzo surface, and it possesses precisely one elliptic fibration. We offer an explicit description of this fibration as well. In the concluding section, we outline several open questions and potential directions for future research. Furthermore, the $p_{\rm T}$ dependence of the $v_2$ for electrons from charm decays is compared with model predictions. We evaluate the performance of two power control strategies: an optimal approach and a binary method. Our findings indicate that the maximum Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) gain achieved by optimal power control over binary power control scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This result contrasts with the scenario where only average power constraints apply, in which the corresponding gain is $\Theta(K)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the GDoF gain of optimal power control relative to fixed power allocation also scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. These conclusions are derived from a novel lower bound on the GDoF, which is established using a combination of information-theoretic and graph-theoretic techniques. Additionally, we present a lower bound on the GDoF for the specific case of a $2 \times 2$ user interference network. This bound is achieved by a binary power control scheme that employs a random linear network coding strategy at the destinations. Finally, we establish that this lower bound is tight for the $2 \times 2$ user interference network. The tightness is proven by constructing a graph that represents the network's GDoF region and applying graph-theoretic methods to determine the region's extreme points. These points correspond to the GDoF values of specific time-sharing schemes, thereby defining the GDoF region. The graph-theoretic approach also enables the calculation of the graph's fractional chromatic number, which equals the network's GDoF. This demonstrates that the GDoF of the $2 \times 2$ user interference network is determined by the fractional chromatic number of a graph with four vertices. Consequently, the GDoF is independent of the specific channel coefficients, provided they are non-zero. Formal concept analysis (FCM) is a mathematical framework used to model knowledge within a specific context, representing it as a network of concepts and their relationships. This study introduces a method for categorizing data by integrating FCM with Dempster-Shafer (DS) theory. The proposed approach involves clustering data into multiple groups, where each group is assigned a belief function derived from the fuzzy membership degrees of its elements. This belief function is subsequently transformed into a categorical concept within FCM. The methodology is demonstrated using a dataset of 1,000 individuals, and the resulting categorization is evaluated through an audit process. The Stitching algorithm, introduced by Bressan et al. (2018), is a method for generating point patterns within a bounded region. It operates by selecting two points uniformly at random and then stitching them together through the application of a stationary, isotropic, and stochastically bounded pair correlation function, denoted as $g$. This paper extends the Stitching algorithm to create non-homogeneous point patterns. We demonstrate that the resulting algorithm is consistent with a specific class of Strauss processes, which are defined by a pair correlation function $g(x) = \exp(-\theta d(x))$, where $\theta$ is a parameter and $d(x)$ represents the Euclidean distance between points. Furthermore, we establish that the algorithm produces patterns that are consistent with any Strauss process, provided the parameter $\theta$ is non-negative. Finally, we present a simulation study comparing the performance of the algorithm against other methods for simulating inhomogeneous Strauss processes. The study indicates that the proposed algorithm performs comparably to other approaches. Additionally, we have made the implementation available in the R package `spathtis`. The package includes a function, `createFromStrauss`, which utilizes the stitching method to generate inhomogeneous point patterns. This function accepts a vector of intensity values and a pair correlation function as inputs. Users can specify the pair correlation function either by providing a function object or by defining it using the formula $g(x) = \exp(-\theta x^{\alpha})$, where $\theta$ and $\alpha$ are parameters. The function also allows for the selection of a Strauss process model from a predefined list of options. We examine a multitasking allocation framework where agents possess multiple tasks, each demanding specific processing. Agents can either dedicate a task to a dedicated processor or assign it to a shared processor that concurrently handles multiple tasks. The shared processor operates at a reduced speed, yet it allows agents to perform other tasks while waiting for dedicated processing. We analyze a random allocation mechanism in which each task is randomly assigned to either a dedicated or shared processor. Our findings indicate that as the number of tasks grows, the allocation becomes asymptotically efficient, meaning the probability of an agent receiving all their tasks approaches one. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the allocation is asymptotically fair, ensuring that the proportion of agents who receive every one of their tasks converges to one across all possible type profiles. Finally, we establish that the allocation is asymptotically strategyproof, implying that the likelihood of an agent being incentivized to misreport their type diminishes to zero as the number of tasks increases. These asymptotic results hold regardless of the specific distribution of types or the number of agents. Additionally, we explore a deterministic allocation mechanism that achieves exact efficiency and fairness for any profile, though it sacrifices strategyproofness. We also present a mechanism that is both strategyproof and ex-post fair, and prove that it converges to efficiency as the number of tasks increases. Our analysis of these mechanisms relies on a novel coupling of the allocation rules. Finally, we extend our framework to a setting with heterogeneous processors, demonstrating that the allocation remains asymptotically efficient, fair, and strategyproof. However, in this heterogeneous scenario, we show that no mechanism can simultaneously achieve exact efficiency and fairness. This result stems from a specific instance where agents have two tasks, one processor is twice as fast as the other, and the number of agents is odd. In this case, at least one agent must inevitably be left with an unfulfilled task. We conclude by discussing the implications of this impossibility result. Universal adversarial examples are engineered to deceive machine learning models across various architectures and training datasets. While prior research has established their existence for classical neural networks, this study investigates their potential within quantum machine learning (QML) models. We demonstrate that universal adversarial instances and perturbations indeed exist for quantum classifiers. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments conducted on both real quantum hardware and simulated environments. Our findings indicate that the required perturbation magnitude is significantly lower than that of other quantum adversarial attack methods. Additionally, we observe that the success rate of our attack remains consistent across different quantum classifiers. These results offer valuable insights for enhancing the robustness of quantum machine learning models. This paper establishes the global well-posedness of the Vlasov-Poisson system within a bounded region featuring reflective boundaries. The proof relies on a novel a priori estimate that demonstrates the uniform boundedness of the electric field in $L^p$ spaces across time. This system is subsequently extended to a broader class of equations, including the Vlasov-Maxwell system and the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck system, under the assumption of an external force. Furthermore, the analysis is generalized to scenarios involving reflective boundaries for the electric field. Finally, the study confirms global well-posedness for the three-dimensional Vlasov-Fokker-Planck system in a bounded domain with reflective boundaries. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive review of existing results regarding global well-posedness in unbounded settings. The methodology developed herein is applicable to other models, such as the Vlasov-Maxwell system, provided the electric field is appropriately modified. However, the current approach does not yield global well-posedness for the Vlasov-Maxwell system in bounded domains. The primary obstacle lies in the lack of a priori estimates for the electric field, which is essential for proving the global existence of weak solutions. Consequently, the global well-posedness of the Vlasov-Maxwell system in bounded domains remains an open problem. This work aims to advance the resolution of this challenge. The article is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the Vlasov-Poisson system with reflective boundaries and its associated initial and boundary conditions; Section 3 presents the global existence of weak solutions; Section 4 derives a priori estimates for the electric field; Section 5 extends these findings to the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck system; and Section 6 offers a detailed discussion of the Vlasov-Maxwell system. Finally, Section 7 reviews relevant results for the Vlasov-Poisson system in unbounded domains. The authors acknowledge the valuable insights and suggestions provided by Professor J. L. V\'{a}zquez. The stable matching problem involves a set of agents with preferences over one another, where the objective is to identify a stable matching. A matching is defined as stable if no two agents can mutually benefit by deviating from their assigned partners. In the standard formulation, agents submit proposals to their top choices, and the resulting matching is determined. However, this process does not guarantee a stable outcome. This paper investigates a scenario where agents can strategically select which proposals to submit. We examine two specific contexts: the college admissions problem, featuring colleges with capacity limits, and the roommate problem, involving indivisible agents. Our primary contribution is a polynomial-time algorithm that enables each agent to choose proposals such that a stable matching is assured. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this algorithm is optimal by proving that, for both problem types, determining whether a stable matching exists is NP-hard when agents are restricted to submitting only a single proposal. Finally, we explore the relationship between the number of proposals an agent must make and the stability of the resulting matching. We establish that, for both problems, there exists a constant $c$ such that if every agent makes at most $c$ proposals, a stable matching is guaranteed to exist. Additionally, we show that for the roommate problem, no constant $c$ can ensure stability if agents are limited to making at most $c$ proposals, provided the number of agents is sufficiently large. This result is derived from a reduction from the clique problem. Finally, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for college admissions that allows each college to select up to two proposals, ensuring a stable matching. This approach is optimal, as we prove that deciding the existence of a stable matching becomes NP-hard when each college is permitted to make at most one proposal. The hardness of this decision problem is established through a reduction from the 3-SAT problem. This work investigates the recovery of a real-valued signal using quadratic measurements. We introduce a novel algorithm, QSRQ, which is computationally efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance. Specifically, QSRQ successfully reconstructs a $K$-sparse signal of length $N$ from $M$ quadratic measurements with a sampling rate of $M/N \approx 2.5K/N$. We provide a comprehensive numerical analysis of laser-induced thermal profiles within liquids, specifically addressing the intricate self-interference patterns generated by these profiles. This approach integrates a heat diffusion model with a refractive index model to simulate the phenomenon. Our findings indicate that the thermal profile is governed by the competition between heat diffusion and the liquid's heat capacity, whereas the refractive index profile depends on the specific absorption depth of the liquid. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the interference pattern can be accurately predicted by calculating the Fourier transform of the thermal profile. These results offer a robust numerical framework for comprehending the complex physics underlying laser-induced thermal effects in liquids. Additionally, we apply this methodology to examine the thermal profile in water, revealing that the interference pattern exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with the laser's power. Finally, we explore the potential for utilizing this self-interference effect in holographic data storage. This work represents the inaugural study to provide a thorough numerical characterization of laser-induced thermal profiles in liquids. This study examines the robustness of a natural language-based extraction system for design discussions, which relies on a manually created taxonomy of discussion topics. We evaluate the extraction results against two distinct sets of 100 design discussions to assess outcome stability. Our findings indicate that while the system successfully identifies the most prevalent topics, it struggles with less common ones. Furthermore, we observe that the system's performance is highly sensitive to variations in the underlying topic taxonomy. These results underscore the critical need for robustness analysis when developing extraction systems based on taxonomies. Finally, we explore potential strategies to enhance the system's resilience to taxonomy variations. This paper introduces H-STREAM, a new analytics pipeline designed for querying big streams and data histories. Built upon the STREAM engine, H-STREAM is a high-performance, scalable, and fault-tolerant system capable of processing and analyzing massive data streams in real-time. It features a flexible query language that supports both stream and data-centric operations, enabling users to query current streams, historical data, or both simultaneously. The system's architecture is designed to handle big data streams and histories, offering a unified query interface for stream processing, data processing, and hybrid stream-data processing. The study details the architecture and implementation of H-STREAM, presents experimental results, and compares its performance against other analytics pipelines. Additionally, the paper explores the applications of H-STREAM within the Internet of Things (IoT) and its potential for big data processing. Finally, the authors outline future research directions, including the development of a distributed query language, the integration of machine learning, and the application of H-STREAM in big data processing. The paper concludes with a summary of the work. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/STREAM-Engine/H-STREAM. We present non-resonant visualizations of top and bottom partner production at the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) and the Future Circular Collider (FCC-ee), which are essential for investigating the Higgs self-coupling. These images are designed to assist experimentalists in identifying the most promising signatures for the HL-LHC and FCC-ee. Additionally, we provide a Python-based toolkit to generate such illustrations, enabling the community to explore these signatures interactively. This resource is available at https://github.com/TopQuarkPhysics/TTbarIllustrator. Our findings indicate that the HL-LHC can probe top partners up to approximately 1.5 TeV and bottom partners up to about 1 TeV. In contrast, the FCC-ee can investigate top partners with masses reaching roughly 1.2 TeV and bottom partners up to approximately 600 GeV. These limits are derived from the sensitivity of the Higgs self-coupling, which is expected to reach 10% at the HL-LHC and 3% at the FCC-ee. Streaming tensor completion (STC) is a powerful method for reconstructing data streams containing missing values. However, current STC techniques struggle with large-scale data due to the high computational costs of operations like SVD and SVD-like updates. To address this, we introduce a novel STC approach that leverages patch tracking to accelerate tensor recovery. Our method begins by decomposing the input tensor into overlapping patches, which are then tracked across successive iterations. During each iteration, these patches are updated using a low-rank approximation derived from their historical data. This strategy significantly reduces computational complexity while maintaining high reconstruction accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions in both speed and accuracy. Furthermore, we apply this technique to a real-world dataset to recover missing data from a large-scale video surveillance system. The successful recovery of missing video frames validates the method's effectiveness and scalability. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/PatchTracking. This paper establishes that the Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}(V)$ associated with traditional Weyl groups $W$ are of finite type. Specifically, when $W$ is a finite group, the dimension of $\mathcal{B}(V)$ equals $|R|$, where $R$ denotes the set of roots in a root system linked to $W$. Conversely, if $W$ is an affine group, the dimension is infinite, and $\mathcal{B}(V)$ possesses the structure of a quantum torus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $\mathcal{B}(V)$ is isomorphic to the quantum torus defined by the Cartan matrix of $W$. Additionally, we examine the case where $W$ is a finite Coxeter group of rank 3, proving that $\mathcal{B}(V)$ is either finite-dimensional or isomorphic to the quantum torus determined by the Cartan matrix of an affine group. Finally, we analyze Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}(V)$ for traditional Weyl groups of rank 4, showing that $\mathcal{B}(V)$ is either finite-dimensional or isomorphic to the quantum torus defined by the Cartan matrix of an affine group of rank 4. In this analysis, we also investigate the scenario where the Nichols algebra is of diagonal type. Notably, the traditional Weyl groups considered here are not limited to those derived from finite-dimensional simple Lie algebras. This work extends the findings of [10] and [11]. We present numerical findings regarding the energy spectrum of two-dimensional, two-way coupled nonlinear wave turbulence systems. Our results confirm the presence of a Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) cascade and demonstrate that the ZK spectrum accurately describes the energy distribution across scales within the inertial range. This paper examines the convergence of the iterative normalization technique for edge weights, originally proposed by Kempe et al. to address the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem. We demonstrate that the iteratively normalized edge weights converge to a maximum weight independent set in any graph where the maximum degree is at most 2. Furthermore, we establish that this iterative approach fails to yield a maximum weight independent set for graphs with a maximum degree of 3. Finally, we present an algorithm that determines whether the iterative normalization method produces a maximum weight independent set in graphs with a maximum degree of at most 3. The runtime of this algorithm is $O(n^3)$, where $n$ represents the number of vertices. Additionally, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm to decide if the iterative normalization yields a maximum weight independent set for line graphs with a maximum degree of at most 4. The runtime for this second algorithm is $O(n^2)$, with $n$ denoting the number of edges in the original graph. Both algorithms are constructive, meaning they generate the maximum weight independent set. We also discuss the relationship between these algorithms and the fractional chromatic number. Finally, we outline an algorithm to verify if the iterative normalization produces a maximum weight independent set for graphs with a maximum degree of at most 5, though this method does not run in polynomial time. The runtime of this third algorithm is $O(n^4)$, where $n$ is the number of vertices in the graph. We also note that this algorithm is constructive. However, we prove that for graphs with a maximum degree of at least 6, the iterative normalization does not necessarily yield a maximum weight independent set. The paper concludes with several open problems. The primary contribution of this work is a novel proof technique that may be applicable to other iterative algorithms. We report the first low-frequency radio observations of the flare star binary system CR Draconis, conducted using the LOFAR telescope over a period of 10.5 years. These observations reveal a persistent, low-frequency radio source at approximately 100 MHz, exhibiting a flat spectrum and a circular polarization fraction exceeding 90%. The source's position aligns with the known position of the binary system, and its flux density remains stable at roughly 10 mJy. We propose that this emission is generated by the electron-cyclotron maser instability within the magnetosphere of the more massive flare star, CR Draconis A. This mechanism is supported by the emission's high circular polarization, low frequency, and long-term stability. Furthermore, the observed emission suggests a magnetic field strength of about 100 G at the star's surface, which is comparable to values found in other flare stars. This detection of maser emission from CR Draconis A is significant because it demonstrates that maser emission can persist for extended durations, a phenomenon previously observed only in the magnetospheres of Jupiter and Saturn. Additionally, the emission's stability indicates that maser emission can remain active for long periods, a characteristic not previously seen in flare stars. These findings offer valuable insights into the magnetospheres of active stars and their interaction with their environments. Finally, the detection of this low-frequency emission from a nearby flare star opens new avenues for studying the magnetospheres of other active stars. This study underscores the necessity of conducting low-frequency observations of flare stars to better understand their magnetospheres and their interactions with surrounding environments. We examine two-dimensional frustrated trimer antiferromagnets using cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our analysis focuses on the phase diagram of the frustrated triangular lattice trimer Heisenberg model, which encompasses both the Rokhsar-Kivelson (RK) and Ising-like phases. By employing a novel cluster update algorithm, we achieve the sampling of large clusters, enabling a precise determination of the phase diagram. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed analysis of the critical exponents at the phase boundaries. Our findings indicate that the critical behavior at the Ising phase boundary aligns with the 2D Ising universality class, while the transition between the RK phase and the paramagnetic phase exhibits a new universality class. Additionally, we explore the potential for extending this methodology to investigate other frustrated magnetic systems. Finally, we apply this approach to the frustrated trimer Heisenberg model on the Kagome lattice, demonstrating that it exhibits a single paramagnetic phase. This result contrasts with the classical model, which displays a rich phase diagram including a Rokhsar-Kivelson phase and a large triangular phase. We attribute this discrepancy to quantum fluctuations, which are more pronounced in the quantum model. These results underscore the necessity of quantum simulations for accurately describing the phase diagrams of frustrated quantum systems. Our methodology is applicable to a broad range of frustrated quantum models. As a demonstration, we also investigate the frustrated square lattice trimer Heisenberg model, revealing a phase diagram characterized by two distinct phases: a paramagnetic phase and a novel phase featuring a non-zero dimerization order parameter. This latter phase is distinct from the RK phase and is not observed in the classical counterpart. We conclude that this phase represents a new universality class. These findings highlight the capability of cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations to elucidate the phase diagrams of frustrated quantum models. We introduce a novel diagnostic tool designed to determine the redshifts of high-redshift galaxies, specifically targeting the detection of the 30 GHz and 100 GHz dust continuum emission lines within the (sub)millimeter spectrum. This method is named "High-z Sudoku" because it relies on the fundamental Sudoku principle that every number must appear exactly once in each row and column. The technique is validated using a sample of 100 galaxies with spectroscopically confirmed redshifts exceeding z=2, where the redshifts are derived from the Cosmic Evolution Survey (CEC) and the James Webb Space Telescope Early Release Science (JWST ERS) programs. Our analysis demonstrates that High-z Sudoku achieves a 90% success rate in correctly identifying redshifts for this sample. Furthermore, we show that the method's performance remains robust even when the input spectral energy distribution (SED) data are noisy or incomplete. Finally, we illustrate how High-z Sudoku can be applied to the recently published ALMA Early Science Large Program (ESLP) sample to determine redshifts for galaxies at z>2.5. This approach enables the identification of dust continuum emission lines at 30 GHz and 100 GHz, which are critical for characterizing the star formation and chemical evolution of galaxies at high redshifts.
